topics.title: Relevant cash flows
topics.summary: A project is judged only on the cash flows that change because we take it. This topic teaches what to count (opportunity costs, erosion, extra working capital), what to ignore (sunk costs, allocated overhead, financing) and the five tax categories that tell you what each cash flow is multiplied by.

topics.title: Operating cash flow
topics.summary: Operating cash flow is the yearly cash a project generates before capital spending and working capital. You will meet four equivalent ways to compute it and see why CCA is added back even though it lowers taxes.

topics.title: Net working capital
topics.summary: Projects tie up cash in inventory and receivables, partly funded by payables. A positive change in NWC is a cash outflow counted in full, and the investment comes back when the project ends.

topics.title: CCA and the tax shield
topics.summary: Canadian tax depreciation (CCA) is declining balance on the undepreciated capital cost (UCC), with a first-year multiplier of 0.5, 1.5 or 1. Each year's CCA saves tax (the shield), and the whole stream can be valued at once with the PV of CCA tax shield formula.

topics.title: Disposal of assets
topics.summary: When a depreciated asset is sold, the proceeds are compared with UCC and the original cost (ACB). The excess up to ACB is recaptured CCA taxed at the full rate, any amount above ACB is a capital gain taxed on half, and a shortfall below UCC is a terminal loss that saves tax.

topics.title: Assembling an NPV
topics.summary: Put the pieces together: after-tax operating flows, CAPEX, working capital, salvage and the PV of the CCA tax shield. The same machinery handles expansions, replacements, cost-cutting proposals, bid prices and the choice of when to sell.

topics.title: EAC with taxes, nominal vs real
topics.summary: Mutually exclusive projects with unequal lives are compared by their equivalent annual cost, computed after tax with PVCCA and salvage. Nominal cash flows are discounted at nominal rates and real cash flows at real rates.

concepts.term: Incremental cash flows and the stand-alone principle
concepts.definition: Incremental cash flows are all the changes in the firm's future after-tax cash flows that are a direct consequence of taking the project: cash flow with the project minus cash flow without it. The stand-alone principle treats them as the cash flows of an imaginary separate firm and values that firm.
concepts.explain: Ask one question of every item: does the firm's cash flow change because we accept this project? If yes, count it after tax and in the year the cash actually moves; if no, ignore it. Once the incremental flows sit on a timeline you discount them like any other cash flows, and a positive NPV means the project adds wealth for the owners.
concepts.example: Prairie Mill's new line adds $600,000 of sales and $280,000 of cash costs but cuts profits on existing products by $120,000 (erosion). Head-office overhead of $90,000 is paid either way. At T = 30% and ignoring CCA: (600,000 − 280,000 − 120,000)(1 − 0.30) = $140,000 per year.
concepts.contrast: Incremental cash flow is not accounting profit: profit contains accruals, allocations and non-cash charges and ignores CAPEX and working capital. It is also not total firm cash flow, which includes flows that happen with or without the project.
concepts.trap: Cue words 'allocated', 'already paid', 'last year', 'head office', 'would have happened anyway' mean drop the item; 'lost sales', 'could be sold or rented', 'extra inventory' mean add it. You can lose marks in both directions: counting what you should not and missing what you should.
concepts.mnemonic: With minus without.
concepts.formula: Incremental CF = CF(with project) − CF(without project)

concepts.term: Sunk, allocated and opportunity costs
concepts.definition: A sunk cost has already been paid (or committed) and cannot change with the decision, so it is counted at zero. An allocated cost is a share of overhead the firm pays anyway and is also counted at zero. An opportunity cost is the most valuable alternative given up, measured at what an owned asset is worth today after tax, and it is counted as an outflow.
concepts.explain: Owned does not mean free. If a project uses land or space the firm could sell or rent, charge the project today's after-tax market value (or the after-tax rent forgone), never the price paid years ago. Money already spent on a study, even a non-refundable one, is gone whatever you decide, so it does not belong in the analysis.
concepts.example: Marlow Aggregates' gravel plant will use land bought nine years ago for $2.8M, now worth $3.4M (tax-free sale). With plant $12.6M and site preparation $0.65M, year 0 = −(3.4 + 12.6 + 0.65) = −$16.65M. The $0.2M environmental assessment paid last year is sunk and ignored.
concepts.contrast: Sunk (past, cannot change, count 0) versus opportunity (a future benefit given up, count at today's value) versus allocated (overhead that does not change, count 0). All three sound like 'costs of the project' but only the opportunity cost is incremental.
concepts.trap: 'Bought six years ago for' is bait: use today's market value. 'Spent last year', 'already paid' or 'non-refundable' means sunk. 'Could otherwise be rented out' means add the after-tax rent forgone. If the sale would be taxed, the opportunity cost is the after-tax amount.
concepts.mnemonic: Sunk is gone; owned is not free.

concepts.term: Side effects and financing costs
concepts.definition: Side effects are changes in the cash flows of the firm's other products caused by the project: erosion (a loss) is subtracted and a synergy or spillover (a gain) is added, both after tax. Financing costs such as interest, dividends and principal repaid are never part of project cash flows.
concepts.explain: Erosion counts only when the lost sales would not have been lost anyway, for example to a competitor. Financing is analyzed separately: the discount rate already charges for the cost of capital, so subtracting interest as well would double count the cost of funds.
concepts.example: A premium cold brew takes $85,000 a year of pre-tax profit from regular iced coffee. At T = 30% the after-tax erosion is −85,000(1 − 0.30) = −$59,500 a year. The interest on the bank loan used to buy the equipment never appears.
concepts.contrast: Erosion (a loss on other products caused by the project) versus an opportunity cost (the best alternative use of an owned asset) versus a financing effect (excluded). Erosion belongs inside the operating cash flow; financing stays outside it.
concepts.trap: Words like 'interest', 'loan' or 'dividend' in the stem are decoys: they never enter the cash flows. 'A competitor would have taken the sales anyway' removes the erosion. Remember to tax-effect side effects.
concepts.mnemonic: Interest never appears.

concepts.term: The five tax categories of cash flows
concepts.definition: Every project cash flow falls into one of five categories: (a) not counted (× 0): sunk and allocated costs; (b) counted in full (× 1): capital expenditure and the change in net working capital; (c) multiplied by (1 − T): revenues and cash expenses; (d) multiplied by T: the CCA tax shield; (e) other tax flows: the sale of depreciated assets (recapture, terminal loss, capital gain).
concepts.explain: The category tells you what a dollar of that item is worth after tax. A dollar of revenue becomes (1 − T) because the firm pays tax on it; a dollar of expense costs only (1 − T) because it is deductible; a dollar of CCA is not paid in cash so it is worth only the tax it saves, T. CAPEX and working capital are cash moved through the balance sheet, so they count in full.
concepts.example: At T = 30%: extra sales of $100,000 are worth $70,000; $150,000 of advertising paid last year is $0 (sunk); selling an asset for $197,000 (cost $590,000, UCC $155,566.41) gives 197,000 − 0.30(197,000 − 155,566.41) = $184,569.92 after tax.
concepts.contrast: Multiplying by (1 − T) versus T is the classic confusion: a cash item (revenue or expense) is multiplied by (1 − T), a non-cash deduction (CCA) by T. CAPEX and NWC look like costs but are not tax-adjusted.
concepts.trap: Taxing CAPEX or NWC; counting a sunk study; using (1 − T) on CCA; forgetting NWC recovery and the tax effects of selling an asset. The sample exam asks for the after-tax value of a revenue, a sunk advertising cost and an asset sale in one question.
concepts.mnemonic: Zero, one, one-minus-T, T, and the sale.

concepts.term: Operating cash flow (OCF)
concepts.definition: OCF = EBIT + D − Tax, where D is the CCA claimed. Equivalent forms: EBIT(1 − T) + D; Net income + D (bottom-up); S − C − Tax (top-down); and (S − C)(1 − T) + T × D (the tax-shield approach).
concepts.explain: OCF is the cash a project generates in a year from running it, before capital spending and working capital. CCA is deducted to find taxable income but added back because no cash left the firm, and it still helps through the tax it saves. Interest never appears. Use whichever form fits the data, since all four must agree.
concepts.contrast: OCF versus net income (OCF adds back D), versus free cash flow (FCF = OCF − CAPEX − change in NWC) and versus EBITDA (before tax). The tax-shield form shows the effect of CCA directly: each extra $1 of CCA raises OCF by T.
concepts.trap: Forgetting to add D back; taxing S − C instead of EBIT; subtracting interest; using D instead of T × D in the shield form; mixing pre-tax and after-tax terms. When the stem gives EBIT, CCA and tax paid, use OCF = EBIT + D − Tax.
concepts.mnemonic: Shield form: after-tax profit plus T times CCA.
concepts.formula: OCF = EBIT + D − Tax = (S − C)(1 − T) + T × D = NI + D

concepts.term: Net working capital (NWC) in a project
concepts.definition: WC = Cash + Inventory + Receivables − Payables (current assets minus current liabilities). A project's change in NWC is NWC_t − NWC_(t-1); a positive change is a cash outflow counted in full (× 1), and the NWC is recovered as an inflow when the project ends.
concepts.explain: A project needs cash on hand, inventory and credit sales, partly financed by suppliers' credit (payables). The firm supplies the difference up front and gets it back when inventory is sold, receivables collected and payables paid. So NWC behaves like a loan to the project, with no tax effect and no CCA.
concepts.example: NWC is $20,000 at t = 0, $25,000 at t = 1 and $22,000 at t = 2, and all of it is released at t = 3. Cash flows from NWC: −20,000, −5,000, +3,000, +22,000. Sample exam Q6: inventory increasing gives a positive change in NWC.
concepts.contrast: Change in NWC versus an expense versus CAPEX: the change in NWC is not tax-deductible and not depreciated (× 1), but unlike CAPEX it is recovered in full at the end. A rise in payables lowers NWC, so it is a cash inflow in the year.
concepts.trap: Positive change in NWC is an outflow, so inventory up, receivables up or cash balances up all use cash; payables up releases cash. Do not multiply NWC by (1 − T) and do not forget the recovery at the end.
concepts.mnemonic: Inventory up, cash out.
concepts.formula: WC = Cash + Inventory + Receivables − Payables; CF_t = −ΔNWC_t

concepts.term: CCA schedule and UCC
concepts.definition: CCA is tax depreciation on a declining balance at the class rate d: CCA_1 = m × d × I0 (m = 0.5, 1.5 or 1), CCA_t = d × UCC_(t-1) for later years, and UCC_t = UCC_(t-1) − CCA_t. The UCC never reaches zero, and the tax saved each year is DTS_t = CCA_t × T_C.
concepts.explain: Build the schedule year by year: claim a percentage of what is left, subtract it from the balance, repeat. Year 1 is special because of the multiplier m; from year 2 on there is no multiplier at all. The UCC at the date of sale is needed for recapture or a terminal loss.
concepts.example: Lecture example: $7,500, d = 30%, AII. CCA_1 = 3,375, UCC_1 = 4,125; CCA_2 = 1,237.50, UCC_2 = 2,887.50; CCA_3 = 866.25; CCA_4 = 606.375; UCC at the start of year 5 = 1,414.875. Closed form: UCC_n = I0(1 − m d)(1 − d)^(n-1).
concepts.contrast: Declining-balance CCA versus straight-line depreciation: CCA each year is d × the remaining UCC, not d × the original cost, so the amounts shrink. CCA versus accounting depreciation: only CCA changes the tax bill.
concepts.trap: Applying 0.5 or 1.5 in every year; using d × I0 every year (straight-line); forgetting that UCC rolls forward; multiplying by (1 − T) instead of T when converting to a shield. Under the half-year rule year 2 has the largest CCA.
concepts.mnemonic: Claim a slice of what is left.
concepts.formula: CCA_1 = m d I0; CCA_t = d × UCC_(t-1); UCC_t = UCC_(t-1) − CCA_t

concepts.term: Half-year rule, AII and the 100% allowance
concepts.definition: The first-year multiplier m scales the CCA on a new asset: 0.5 under the half-year rule, 1.5 under the Accelerated Investment Incentive (AII), and 1.0 for an asset already being depreciated or when the question states a full first-year rate. In the PV of CCA tax shield it becomes the factor (1 + 0.5k)/(1 + k), (1.5k + 1)/(1 + k) or 1.
concepts.explain: Tax law changes, and the professor says to be capable of handling any rules: read the question and use the multiplier it states, defaulting to the half-year rule when nothing is said. The multiplier acts on d × I0 in year 1 only. A faster first-year claim brings the tax saving forward, so the PV is larger.
concepts.example: I0 = $120,000, d = 30%, T = 25%. Half-year: CCA_1 = 18,000, DTS = 4,500. AII: CCA_1 = 54,000, DTS = 13,500. With k = 10% the PVCCA factors are 0.9545 (half-year), 1.0000 (100%) and 1.0455 (AII).
concepts.contrast: Half-year (m = 0.5) versus AII (m = 1.5): AII front-loads CCA and gives the higher PV. An asset the firm already owns has already used its first-year adjustment, so its factor is 1.
concepts.trap: Applying m every year, picking the wrong factor in PVCCA (0.5 versus 1.5 regime), or applying m to a continuing asset. Check whether the asset is new this year or already depreciating.
concepts.mnemonic: Half: 0.5. Incentive: 1.5. Old asset: 1.

concepts.term: CCA tax shield (DTS)
concepts.definition: The depreciation tax shield in year t is DTS_t = CCA_t × T_C, the tax saved because CCA is deductible. It is called a shield because it shields income from tax, reducing the tax bill, provided the firm has enough other taxable income.
concepts.explain: CCA is not paid in cash, so its only cash effect is the tax it saves: T cents per dollar of CCA. Because CCA declines with UCC, the DTS shrinks every year. The size of the shield rises with the tax rate and with how quickly CCA is claimed.
concepts.contrast: DTS versus CCA: CCA is a deduction measured in dollars of income, the DTS is the cash tax it saves (CCA × T). A cash expense is multiplied by (1 − T) because cash is paid; CCA by T because nothing is paid.
concepts.trap: Forgetting to multiply CCA by T; using (1 − T); reusing year-1 CCA in later years; assuming a shield exists even though the firm has no other taxable income.
concepts.mnemonic: Shield: CCA times T.

concepts.term: PV of the CCA tax shield (PVCCA)
concepts.definition: PV_CCA = (I0 d T_C)/(k + d) × {1, (1 + 0.5k)/(1 + k), (1.5k + 1)/(1 + k)} − (S_N d T_C)/(k + d) × 1/(1 + k)^N. The first factor is chosen by the regime (100%, half-year, AII); the last term is used only if the asset is sold in year N for S_N.
concepts.explain: The shield CCA × T_C shrinks at rate d each year, so it is a growing perpetuity with g = −d: PV = first shield/(k − g) = CCA_1 T_C/(k + d). The half-year and AII factors adjust for the first year's different claim. If the asset is sold in year N, CCA on it stops, so subtract the PV of the tail lost: S_N d T_C/(k + d) discounted N years. This is the PV of CCA only; the disposal tax is separate.
concepts.example: Seminar 5: I0 = $110,000 (equipment plus installation), d = 20%, T = 40%, k = 10%, AII, sold in 6 years for $17,000. PVCCA = 30,666.67 − 2,558.95 = $28,107.72.
concepts.contrast: k + d versus k − d: the shield declines, so it is d added to k. S_N versus UCC_N in the last term: use the sale price S_N. Sold versus kept: omit the last term when the asset is not sold and the pool stays open.
concepts.trap: Using k − d; wrong first-year factor; salvage term not discounted; UCC instead of S_N; dropping the term when the asset is sold or keeping it when the pool stays open. Also never discount PVCCA again: it is already a present value.
concepts.mnemonic: Shield over (k plus d), minus the tail after the sale.

concepts.term: Net acquisitions rule and net salvage
concepts.definition: When assets are bought and sold in the same CCA class in the same year, the first-year rule applies to net acquisitions = additions − min(original cost, selling price) of the disposals. In a replacement analysis the PVCCA uses the net acquisition cost (new cost − old resale today) as I0 and the net salvage (new salvage − old salvage) as S_N.
concepts.explain: Selling the old machine takes its capital cost out of the pool, so the pool grows only by the net amount. If the net acquisition is positive, apply the half-year or 1.5 rule to it; if it is negative, no adjustment is made. Net salvage can be negative, in which case the salvage term adds to PVCCA.
concepts.example: Dickerson: new machine $280,000, old resale $60,000: net acquisition = $220,000. Salvage in 4 years $18,000 (new) and $10,000 (old): net salvage = $8,000. With d = 25%, T = 40%, k = 11%, AII: PVCCA = $62,675.29.
concepts.contrast: Net acquisition cost (the I0 of the PVCCA) versus net salvage (the S_N): one is today, one is at the end. Net acquisition versus gross cost of the new asset: using the full $280,000 overstates the shield.
concepts.trap: Using the full purchase price; using the original cost or UCC of the old asset instead of the lesser of cost and proceeds; subtracting salvages in the wrong direction; forgetting that net salvage may be negative.
concepts.mnemonic: New minus old, today and at the end.
concepts.formula: Net acquisitions = additions − min(original cost, POD); net salvage = S_N(new) − S_N(old)

concepts.term: Recapture of CCA and terminal loss
concepts.definition: At disposal, compare the proceeds of disposition (POD) with UCC and ACB (the adjusted cost base, i.e. cost plus acquisition expense). The amount min(ACB, POD) − UCC is taxed at the full rate T when positive (recapture of CCA) and is a tax saving T × (UCC − POD) when negative (terminal loss).
concepts.explain: Recapture means we claimed too much CCA relative to what the asset really lost, so CRA takes the extra back as income. A terminal loss means we claimed too little, so the unclaimed balance is deducted. Either way the tax flow is T times the difference between the lesser of ACB and POD and UCC.
concepts.example: Lecture example: sell the $7,500 asset in year 5 for $3,000 at T = 38%; UCC = 1,414.875. Recapture = 3,000 − 1,414.875 = 1,585.125; tax = 0.38 × 1,585.125 = 602.35; after-tax proceeds = $2,397.65. Check: total tax saved = T × (cost − proceeds) = 0.38 × 4,500 = $1,710.
concepts.contrast: Recapture (POD above UCC, taxed at T) versus terminal loss (POD below UCC, tax saved) versus capital gain (POD above ACB, taxed on half). Only the part of POD up to ACB can be recapture.
concepts.trap: Taxing the whole POD, using POD − ACB as the recapture, getting the sign of a terminal loss wrong (it is a refund), or forgetting that recapture uses min(ACB, POD). A pool that stays open has no immediate recapture or terminal loss.
concepts.mnemonic: Compare POD with UCC: above is tax, below is refund.
concepts.formula: CF_AT = POD − T[min(ACB, POD) − UCC] − 0.5 T max(POD − ACB, 0)

concepts.term: Capital gain and the after-tax disposal cash flow CF_AT
concepts.definition: Any proceeds above the ACB are a capital gain, and only 50% of the gain is taxable. The after-tax disposal cash flow is CF_AT = POD − T × [min(ACB, POD) − UCC] − 0.5 × T × max(POD − ACB, 0).
concepts.explain: Work in three steps: the recapture or terminal loss relative to UCC (capped at ACB), the capital gain relative to ACB, then subtract the tax from POD. The 50% inclusion applies only to the gain above cost. Many exam assets are sold below cost, so the capital-gain term is zero.
concepts.contrast: Capital gain (above ACB, half taxed) versus recapture (between UCC and ACB, fully taxed). Do not compute a gain relative to UCC.
concepts.trap: Taxing recapture at 50%, taxing a gain that is not there because POD < ACB, or measuring the gain from UCC. The formula is on the sheet; the work is in finding min and max correctly.
concepts.mnemonic: Gain above cost: half-taxed.
concepts.formula: CF_AT = POD − T[min(ACB, POD) − UCC] − 0.5 T max(POD − ACB, 0)

concepts.term: Pool stays open versus pool closes
concepts.definition: If other assets remain in the CCA class (the pool stays open), selling an asset triggers no recapture or terminal loss: the proceeds simply reduce UCC and CCA continues on the smaller pool. If the sale leaves the class empty (the pool closes), the remaining UCC is compared with POD and the CF_AT formula applies immediately.
concepts.explain: Tax law pools assets by class, so the sale of one asset only matters on its own when it is the last one. With an open pool the effect shows up through the lost future CCA on the sale price (the salvage term in PVCCA). With a closed pool the whole difference between UCC and POD is taxed or deducted now.
concepts.example: A $20,000 machine in a class that still holds other assets is sold for $4,000: the firm receives $4,000 and UCC of the pool falls by $4,000. If it were the last asset in the class and UCC were $9,000, a terminal loss of $5,000 would save T × 5,000 in tax.
concepts.contrast: Open pool (no immediate tax on the sale, shield continues on a smaller base) versus closed pool (immediate recapture or terminal loss, CCA stops).
concepts.trap: Applying recapture or terminal loss to an asset whose class stays open; ignoring the terminal loss when the class closes; forgetting which case the question describes (look for 'no assets left in the class').
concepts.mnemonic: Last one out turns off the lights.
concepts.formula: Open: CF = POD, UCC falls by POD. Closed: CF_AT formula

concepts.term: Expansion project NPV
concepts.definition: NPV of an expansion = CF0 + PV of after-tax operating flows + PV of NWC and salvage flows + PV_CCA, where CF0 = −(CAPEX + initial NWC + opportunity costs), operating flows are (S − C)(1 − T) including erosion, and PV_CCA is added (not discounted again).
concepts.explain: Follow the order: (1) incremental cash flows (drop sunk costs, add land and erosion); (2) after-tax revenue less costs each year; (3) CAPEX and NWC at t = 0, changes in NWC after, recovery at the end; (4) salvage; (5) discount at k; (6) add PVCCA with the right first-year factor and the salvage term; (7) accept if NPV > 0.
concepts.example: Seminar 6 tractor plant: CAPEX $170M, land $10M, NWC $3M then 5% of sales, sales $100M less $10M erosion, costs $45M, T = 35%, d = 10%, k = 12%, salvage $100M at year 10, AII. NPV = 14.29 + 28.49 − 5.12 = $37.66M, so take the project.
concepts.contrast: Expansion versus replacement: an expansion adds a new asset and has no old asset to sell, so there is no net-acquisition adjustment. The PVCCA is added once, undiscounted again.
concepts.trap: Counting the sunk feasibility study; forgetting the land opportunity cost; recovering NWC twice; discounting PVCCA again; using interest. Also check the erosion: the lost $10M of sales reduces after-tax income.
concepts.mnemonic: Flows, NWC, salvage, then shield.
concepts.formula: NPV = CF0 + PV(after-tax flows, NWC, salvage) + PV_CCA

concepts.term: Replacement project NPV
concepts.definition: A replacement NPV uses incremental flows: the net acquisition cost (new cost − old resale today) at t = 0, the incremental savings or sales after tax, the change in NWC, the net salvage (new − old) at the end, and PV_CCA computed on the net acquisition cost and net salvage.
concepts.explain: Selling the old machine today means we do not get its future salvage, so the old machine's end-of-life value is an opportunity cost netted against the new machine's salvage. Everything is a difference between the 'replace' and 'keep' worlds.
concepts.example: Dickerson (Seminar 6): net acquisition $220,000, extra sales $85,000 to $70,000, NWC 10% of sales, T = 40%, k = 11%, d = 25%, AII, net salvage $8,000. NPV = −$2,075, so do not replace. Simple replacement: −85,000 + savings + net salvage −10,000 + PVCCA gives NPV = $47,867.15, so replace.
concepts.contrast: Replacement versus expansion: a replacement has an old asset whose resale and salvage change the numbers (net acquisition, net salvage). Replacement versus cost cutting: savings are the revenue-like benefit of the new machine.
concepts.trap: Using the full price of the new machine; forgetting that net salvage may be negative; treating the old machine's book value as relevant; ignoring the old machine's lost CCA.
concepts.mnemonic: New minus old, everywhere.
concepts.formula: NPV = −net acquisition + PV(after-tax savings) + PV(net salvage) + PV_CCA(net acquisition, net salvage)

concepts.term: Cost-cutting proposals and required savings
concepts.definition: A cost-cutting proposal has no sales: the benefit is the after-tax saving, (saving)(1 − T) per year. The required pre-tax saving sets NPV = 0: required after-tax annual saving = (outlay − PV_CCA − PV of other flows) / annuity factor, then pre-tax saving = that / (1 − T).
concepts.explain: Treat a cost saving like revenue: it is taxed, so only (1 − T) of it reaches the firm. To find the break-even saving, collect every known present value, back out the annuity that makes NPV zero, and then un-tax it.
concepts.example: Equipment $500,000, d = 20%, T = 35%, k = 10%, 5 years, half-year rule, no salvage. PVCCA = $111,363.64; required after-tax saving = (500,000 − PVCCA)/3.790787 = $102,521.29; required pre-tax saving = 102,521.29/0.65 = $157,725.07.
concepts.contrast: Cost cutting versus expansion: no revenue, so the whole benefit is the tax-adjusted saving. Required saving (NPV = 0 solve) versus NPV of a given saving.
concepts.trap: Forgetting to divide by (1 − T); dividing by N instead of the annuity factor; forgetting the CCA shield or the salvage; multiplying the pre-tax saving by T.
concepts.mnemonic: Back out the annuity, then un-tax.
concepts.formula: Required pre-tax saving = [(outlay − PV_CCA − other PVs) / annuity factor] / (1 − T)

concepts.term: Bid price and break-even revenue
concepts.definition: The minimum bid price makes NPV = 0: PV the known pieces (CAPEX, NWC, salvage, PV_CCA), solve the required after-tax operating cash flow as an annuity, divide by (1 − T), add back costs and divide by the number of units.
concepts.explain: A contractor asks: what is the lowest price at which this job still earns the required return? Treat NPV = 0 as the break-even, back out the after-tax net revenue each year, then un-tax it and add the costs to reach the sales dollars and the price per unit.
concepts.example: SM 10-24 (which applies no first-year factor): initial cost $1,300,000, salvage $650,000 in 3 years, NWC $340,000 recovered, d = 20%, T = 36%, k = 20%, 89 systems a year with variable cost $96,000. Required after-tax operating income = $427,628.57 per year; sales = $9,212,169.64; price at least $103,507.52 per system.
concepts.contrast: Bid price versus NPV of a given price: the bid price is the zero-NPV price, a minimum, not a forecast. Accounting break-even would ignore the time value of money and the required return.
concepts.trap: Forgetting to divide by (1 − T); dividing by N rather than the annuity factor; leaving out the CCA shield or the NWC recovery; stopping at net revenue and not adding back costs.
concepts.mnemonic: NPV zero, un-tax, add costs, divide by units.
concepts.formula: Required after-tax OCF = −(PV of other flows)/annuity factor; price = [OCF/(1 − T) + costs]/Q

concepts.term: Timing of sale and the opportunity cost of the lost shield
concepts.definition: To decide whether to sell an asset now or keep it, compute the NPV at the decision date of selling: the after-tax proceeds CF_AT minus the present value (at that date) of the CCA tax shields we would have kept, d × UCC × T/(k + d).
concepts.explain: Selling stops the CCA tax shield, so the lost shield is an opportunity cost of the sale. Value the remaining shield as a growing perpetuity declining at d from the date of sale, subtract it from the after-tax cash we receive, and sell only if the result is positive.
concepts.example: Lecture example: sell the $7,500 asset in year 5 for $3,000 (T = 38%, k = 10%, d = 30%). CF_AT = $2,397.65; the lost shield at year 5 has PV = 0.38 × 0.30 × 1,414.875/(0.10 + 0.30) = $403.24; NPV at t = 5 is $1,994.41, so selling is better.
concepts.contrast: Selling versus holding: the same asset, two worlds. Compare the after-tax cash received with the PV of the lost future tax shields (and any future salvage).
concepts.trap: Ignoring the lost shield; using the original cost instead of UCC at the sale date; forgetting the disposal tax.
concepts.mnemonic: Sale cash minus lost shield.
concepts.formula: NPV_N(sell) = CF_AT − d × UCC_N × T/(k + d)

concepts.term: Equivalent annual cost with taxes
concepts.definition: EAC = (PV of costs, after tax, including PV_CCA and salvage) / annuity factor(k, N). With unequal lives and replacement, the project with the lower EAC (equivalently, the higher EAV) is preferred.
concepts.explain: Compute each option's total PV of costs: initial outlay, after-tax operating costs, salvage, and the PVCCA benefit. Divide by the annuity factor for its own life to get an annual cost. Pick the lowest annual cost.
concepts.example: Seminar 6 cars: Civil PV of costs −$17,663.79 over 4 years gives EAC −$5,815; Chevalier −$15,547 over 3 years gives EAC −$6,473. Choose the Civil.
concepts.contrast: EAC versus raw NPV: comparing PVs with unequal lives is wrong. EAC versus CCR (NPV to infinity): same ranking, different scale.
concepts.trap: Comparing PVs of different lives; using the wrong annuity factor N; leaving the tax shield out; wrong sign (costs are negative).
concepts.mnemonic: Annualize before comparing.

concepts.term: Nominal versus real cash flows and rates
concepts.definition: Discount nominal cash flows at the nominal rate and real cash flows at the real rate. The rates are linked by (1 + R_nom) = (1 + R_inf)(1 + R_real), and a nominal cash flow in year i converts to real by dividing by (1 + R_inf)^i.
concepts.explain: Inflation inflates the cash flows as well as the required return. If the cash flows already include inflation they are nominal and need a nominal rate; if they are in today's dollars they are real and need the real rate. Never mix them.
concepts.example: Nominal rate 13%, inflation 3%: real rate = 1.13/1.03 − 1 = 9.7087%. Discounting the real cash flows at 9.7087% gives the same PV as discounting the nominal cash flows at 13%.
concepts.contrast: Nominal versus real: the PV is the same if the pairing is consistent, but EACs differ because the annuity factors use different rates.
concepts.trap: Discounting real flows at nominal rates (or the reverse); subtracting inflation from the rate instead of dividing; forgetting to convert a CPI-linked flow.
concepts.mnemonic: Nominal with nominal, real with real.
concepts.formula: (1 + R_nom) = (1 + R_inf)(1 + R_real); CF_real,i = CF_nom,i/(1 + R_inf)^i

activities.title: Sort the cash flow by its tax treatment
activities.prompt: Drag each item to the multiplier that gives its after-tax effect.

items.text: A feasibility study paid last year
Head-office overhead allocated to the project but paid anyway
Purchase of equipment (CAPEX)
Increase in inventory at project start (change in NWC)
Recovery of NWC at the end of the project
Additional sales revenue
Extra wages paid to project staff
Annual labour savings from a new machine
CCA claimed on the equipment
Depreciation (CCA) on a delivery truck bought for the project
Market study fee that is non-refundable and already paid
Cost of materials used in production

activities.explanation: Sunk and allocated costs are × 0, CAPEX and NWC are × 1 (already after-tax money moved through the balance sheet), revenues and cash expenses or savings are × (1 − T), and CCA is × T because it is a non-cash deduction whose only cash effect is the tax saved.

activities.title: Order the steps of a project NPV
activities.prompt: Put the steps of the NPV of an expansion project in the right order.
items: List the incremental cash flows: drop sunk and allocated costs, add opportunity costs and erosion
Compute after-tax operating flows each year: (S − C)(1 − T)
Add CAPEX and initial NWC at t = 0, the changes in NWC each year and the NWC recovery at the end
Add the salvage or disposal cash flow at the end
Discount all of these flows at k to get their PV
Add the PV of the CCA tax shield (with the right first-year factor and salvage term) without discounting it again
Sum to NPV and accept the project if NPV > 0
activities.explanation: First decide what counts, then put each category on the timeline, discount, add the already-discounted PVCCA once, and apply the NPV rule.

activities.title: Match the symbol to its meaning
activities.prompt: Match each term from the disposal and tax shield formulas with its meaning.

pairs.right: Adjusted cost base: cost plus acquisition expense
Proceeds of disposition: the sale value
Undepreciated capital cost: cost less CCA claimed
Accelerated Investment Incentive: 1.5 × d × I0 in year 1
POD below UCC when the class closes: tax saved
POD above UCC (up to ACB): taxed at the full rate

activities.explanation: These are the Canadian disposal and CCA terms from the review list; ACB, POD and UCC drive the CF_AT formula and DTS drives the PVCCA.

activities.title: Order the disposal calculation
activities.prompt: Put the steps of the after-tax cash flow from selling a depreciated asset in order.
items: Roll the CCA schedule forward to find UCC at the date of sale
Compare POD with ACB and compute min(ACB, POD)
Recapture (or terminal loss) = min(ACB, POD) − UCC
Capital gain = max(POD − ACB, 0), of which 50% is taxable
Tax = T × recapture + 0.5 × T × capital gain
activities.explanation: UCC comes first because everything is measured against it; the capital gain only exists above ACB; CF_AT subtracts the total tax from the proceeds.

activities.title: Pick the first-year regime
activities.prompt: Drag each situation to the first-year multiplier (or PVCCA factor) it calls for.

items.text: A new press bought this year; the question says 'half-year rule'
A new van; the question says 'Accelerated Investment Incentive applies'
A machine the firm has owned and depreciated for three years (remaining shield)
A new asset where no rule is mentioned (default)
PVCCA first-year factor (1.5k + 1)/(1 + k)
PVCCA first-year factor (1 + 0.5k)/(1 + k)
A question that says the full first-year rate is allowed

activities.explanation: The multiplier m is set by the rule the question states: 0.5 by default, 1.5 under the AII, and 1.0 for an asset that has already used its first-year adjustment.

activities.title: Match the disposal situation to its tax result
activities.prompt: Match each sale situation with its tax treatment.

pairs.right: Recapture up to ACB at full rate, plus a capital gain taxed on half
Recapture of POD − UCC at the full rate, no capital gain

pairs.left: POD < UCC and the class closes
pairs.right: Terminal loss: tax saved on the shortfall

pairs.left: Asset sold, other assets remain in the class
pairs.right: No immediate recapture or loss; UCC falls by POD

activities.explanation: Compare POD with UCC and ACB. A pool that stays open absorbs the sale; a pool that closes settles the difference at once.

formulas.name: Working capital
formulas.formula: WC = Cash + Inventory + Receivables − Payables = Current assets − Current liabilities
formulas.when: To find NWC balances and the change in them.
formulas.trap: Payables subtract: a rise in payables lowers NWC.

formulas.name: Cash flow from NWC
formulas.formula: ΔNWC_t = NWC_t − NWC_(t-1); project cash flow = −ΔNWC_t; recovery at the end = +NWC
formulas.when: Whenever NWC is invested up front or as a % of sales.
formulas.trap: A positive change is an outflow, counted in full, and recovered at the end.

formulas.name: OCF from EBIT
formulas.when: When EBIT, CCA and tax are known.
formulas.trap: Add D back; tax is on EBIT, not on S − C.

formulas.name: OCF tax-shield form
formulas.when: When sales, costs, CCA and T are known; shows the CCA shield directly.
formulas.trap: The shield is T × D, not D and not (1 − T) × D.

formulas.name: OCF bottom-up and top-down
formulas.formula: OCF = NI + D = S − C − Tax
formulas.when: When net income or the tax paid is the starting point.
formulas.trap: Interest never appears in project cash flows.

formulas.name: Free cash flow
formulas.formula: FCF = EBIT(1 − T) + D&A − CAPEX − ΔWC
formulas.when: Yearly project cash flow after CAPEX and working capital.
formulas.trap: FCF = OCF − CAPEX − ΔNWC; do not subtract interest.

formulas.name: CCA schedule
formulas.formula: CCA_1 = m d I0 (m = 0.5, 1.5, 1.0); CCA_t = d UCC_(t-1); UCC_t = UCC_(t-1) − CCA_t
formulas.when: Year-by-year CCA and UCC at the sale date.
formulas.trap: m applies in year 1 only; later years use d × the opening UCC, not d × I0.

formulas.name: CCA tax shield
formulas.when: Cash tax saved in year t.

formulas.name: PV of the CCA tax shield
formulas.when: Lump the whole stream of tax savings into one present value.
formulas.trap: k + d not k − d; choose the first-year factor; S_N is the sale price and the term is discounted N years; omit it if nothing is sold.

formulas.name: Base PVCCA (growing perpetuity)
formulas.formula: PV_CCA = CCA_1 T_C/(k + d) = I0 d T_C/(k + d)
formulas.when: 100% case: asset already being depreciated; also the PV at a sale date of the shield lost.
formulas.trap: It is Gordon growth with g = −d.

formulas.name: Net acquisitions and net salvage
formulas.formula: Net acquisitions = additions − min(original cost, POD); net salvage = S_N(new) − S_N(old)
formulas.when: Replacement in the same class in the same year.
formulas.trap: Use net amounts in PVCCA; net salvage can be negative.

formulas.name: After-tax disposal cash flow
formulas.formula: CF_AT = POD − T × [min(ACB, POD) − UCC] − 50% × T × max(POD − ACB, 0)
formulas.when: After-tax cash from selling a depreciated asset.
formulas.trap: min(ACB, POD) − UCC may be negative (terminal loss refund); the capital gain exists only above ACB and only half is taxed.

formulas.name: Assembled project NPV
formulas.formula: NPV = CF0 + PV(after-tax flows) + PV(NWC, salvage) + PV_CCA
formulas.trap: PVCCA is already a present value; do not discount it again.

formulas.name: Required saving and bid price
formulas.formula: Required after-tax OCF = −(PV of all other flows)/annuity factor; pre-tax saving = OCF/(1 − T); price = [OCF/(1 − T) + costs]/Q
formulas.when: Set NPV = 0 and solve for the saving or the price.
formulas.trap: Divide by (1 − T) and by the annuity factor, not by N.

formulas.name: Value at the sale date of the lost shield
formulas.formula: NPV_N(sell) = CF_AT − d × UCC_N × T/(k + d)
formulas.trap: The lost shield is an opportunity cost of selling.

formulas.name: Equivalent annual cost
formulas.formula: EAC = PV of costs / annuity factor(k, N), annuity factor = [1 − (1 + k)^(-N)]/k
formulas.trap: Use each option's own N; costs are negative; include PVCCA and salvage.

formulas.name: Nominal and real rates
formulas.when: Convert between nominal and real discount rates.

formulas.name: Real cash flow
formulas.when: Convert a nominal flow to today's dollars.
formulas.trap: Real flows pair with the real rate only.

questions.stem: An incremental cash flow for a project is best described as:
options: the change in the firm's total after-tax cash flows that results directly from accepting the project
the project's accounting net income after a share of head-office costs
all after-tax cash flows the firm will receive in the years the project is running
the project's revenue less its cash expenses, before tax
questions.explanation: Incremental cash flow is cash flow with the project minus cash flow without it, after tax. Net income mixes accruals and allocations, total firm cash flow includes flows that would happen anyway, and revenue less cost before tax ignores the tax that really leaves the firm.

questions.stem: To value a proposed brewery expansion, an analyst puts only the cash flows that the expansion causes on a timeline and values them as if they belonged to a separate, imaginary firm. This approach is called the:
options: net acquisitions rule
stand-alone principle
equivalent annual cost method
capital rationing rule
questions.explanation: The stand-alone principle says that once the incremental cash flows are identified you can treat them as the cash flows of a stand-alone firm and value that firm with NPV.

questions.stem: Which list contains only incremental cash flows for Cascade Cycles' new e-bike line?
options: Revenue from the new e-bike, the e-bike's share of head-office rent, cost of the extra assembly staff
Revenue from the new e-bike, the market-study fee paid last year, cost of the extra assembly staff
Revenue from the new e-bike, lost sales of the older model, cost of the extra assembly staff
Revenue from the new e-bike, interest on the loan funding the line, cost of the extra assembly staff
questions.explanation: Lost sales of the older model are erosion, which changes the firm's cash flow. The other lists contain an allocated cost that is paid anyway, a sunk cost already paid, and a financing cost; none of these changes with the decision.

questions.stem: How do a project's incremental cash flows differ from its accounting net income?
options: Incremental flows are measured before tax, while net income is measured after tax and interest
Incremental flows exclude working capital and capital spending, while net income includes both
They are the same figure, except that incremental flows are reported at year-end
Incremental flows count only after-tax cash changes caused by the project; net income includes accruals, non-cash charges and allocations
questions.explanation: Incremental cash flows are after tax, include CAPEX and working capital, and ignore allocations. Net income is an accrual measure that includes depreciation and allocated costs and ignores CAPEX and working capital.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an incremental cash flow of launching a new product line?
options: An allocated share of the CEO's salary, paid whether or not the line launches
Extra inventory and receivables the new line requires
The after-tax value of an owned building that could otherwise be sold
Profit lost on an existing product that customers switch away from
questions.explanation: An allocated cost does not change with the decision, so its incremental cost is zero. Extra inventory (working capital), the opportunity cost of the building and erosion all change the firm's cash flow.

questions.stem: Why must each incremental flow be recorded in the year the cash actually moves rather than the year it is earned in the accounts?
options: Tax law requires every project to be reported on a cash basis
NPV discounts cash by its date, so timing changes present value
Accrual dates are always unknown for new projects
Discount rates apply only to accounting profit
questions.explanation: The time value of money works on dates of cash, so a sale booked in year 1 but collected in year 2 must be placed in year 2 (or its receivable treated as working capital).

questions.stem: Incremental cash flows are measured after tax.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Taxes are a real cash outflow, so every revenue, expense and saving is stated after tax: revenues and expenses at (1 − T), CCA at T.

questions.stem: The relevant cash flows for a project are the _____ cash flows: the changes in the firm's future cash flows that are a direct consequence of taking the project.
options: accounting
average
incremental
allocated
questions.explanation: Incremental cash flows are the with-versus-without changes. Accounting and allocated figures are not cash changes caused by the project.

questions.stem: An analyst reports a project NPV of +$40,000. It already deducts the present value ($120,000, after tax) of head-office overhead that the firm pays in full whether or not the project goes ahead. What is the correct reading?
options: The NPV is correct, because a project must cover its share of every firm cost
Removing the overhead gives NPV = −$80,000, so the project should be rejected
Removing the overhead changes the NPV only if the project is financed with debt
Overhead is not incremental; removing it gives NPV = +$160,000, so the project looks better
questions.explanation: Allocated overhead that does not change with the decision is not incremental. NPV rises by the $120,000 that was wrongly charged: 40,000 + 120,000 = $160,000. The decision (accept) is unchanged but the value added is understated.

questions.stem: Without a proposed project a firm expects after-tax cash flows of $1,150,000 a year; with it, $1,420,000 a year. Which annual figure should be discounted in the project's NPV?
options: $270,000, the difference between the two
$1,420,000, the cash flow with the project
$1,150,000, the cash flow without the project
$2,570,000, the two added together
questions.explanation: Incremental cash flow is with minus without: 1,420,000 − 1,150,000 = $270,000. Only that change is caused by the project.

questions.stem: Prairie Mill's new oat-flour line adds $600,000 of annual sales and $280,000 of cash costs. It also cuts profit on existing products by $120,000 a year (erosion). Head-office overhead of $90,000 a year is allocated to the line but is paid whether or not it launches. The tax rate is 30%; ignore CCA. What is the line's annual incremental after-tax cash flow?
solution: Allocated overhead is not incremental: ignore the $90,000.

errors.label: Charged the allocated overhead
errors.explain: The overhead is paid either way, so it is not incremental.

errors.label: Ignored the lost profit on existing products
errors.explain: Erosion is a real loss of cash flow caused by the project and must be subtracted.

errors.label: Left the flow before tax
errors.explain: Every incremental flow is stated after tax: multiply by (1 − T).

questions.explanation: Count the new sales, the new costs and the erosion; drop the allocated overhead; then apply (1 − T) to the net operating flow.

questions.stem: Kestrel Foods will buy a $480,000 packaging line, pay $20,000 to have it delivered and installed (capitalized into its cost) and tie up $35,000 of extra working capital at t = 0. A $12,000 feasibility study was paid last quarter. The line goes into floor space the firm owns and has no other use for. What is the incremental cash flow at t = 0?

steps.label: t = 0 incremental cash flow = −(installed cost + NWC)

solution: The $12,000 study is sunk; the unused space has no opportunity cost.

errors.label: Included the feasibility study
errors.explain: The study was paid last quarter; the decision cannot change it.

errors.label: Left out the installation cost
errors.explain: Delivery and installation are part of the capital cost of the line.

errors.label: Left out the extra working capital
errors.explain: Working capital tied up at t = 0 is a cash outflow counted in full.

questions.explanation: At t = 0 the incremental outlay is the installed cost plus the working capital; the sunk study and the free-to-use space contribute nothing.

questions.stem: A Kestrel Foods project needs equipment costing $400,000 and $30,000 of working capital at t = 0. It then yields incremental after-tax operating cash flow of $190,000 a year for 3 years (already net of erosion; a $15,000 study paid last month is excluded). The working capital is recovered at t = 3. Ignore CCA and salvage. At 12% per annum, what is the NPV?

steps.label: PV of the three operating flows
PV of the NWC recovery at t = 3

errors.label: Subtracted the sunk study
errors.explain: The $15,000 study is already paid and is not incremental.

errors.label: Never recovered the working capital
errors.explain: The working capital is released when the project ends, an inflow at t = 3.

errors.label: Used a 4-year annuity
errors.explain: The operating flows last 3 years, so the annuity factor has N = 3.

questions.explanation: Discount the incremental flows: outlay and NWC now, a 3-year annuity of after-tax operating flow, and the NWC recovery at the end.

questions.stem: Cascade Cycles' new e-bike line will sell 4,000 units at $2,400. About 1,100 of those buyers would otherwise have bought the older model at $1,800. The line also lifts accessory sales by $150,000. What is the line's incremental annual revenue?
questions.explanation: Incremental revenue = new sales 9,600,000 − lost older-model sales 1,980,000 (1,100 × $1,800, the old price) + accessories 150,000 = $7,770,000. $9,750,000 ignores erosion; $7,110,000 values the lost sales at the new price; $7,620,000 ignores the accessory spill-over.

questions.stem: Hollis Hardware's new tool line adds $850,000 of annual sales and $410,000 of cash operating costs. Head-office overhead of $70,000 is allocated to the line but is paid in full either way. The tax rate is 35%; ignore CCA. What is the incremental annual after-tax cash flow?
questions.explanation: Incremental flow = (850,000 − 410,000)(1 − 0.35) = $286,000. $240,500 charges the allocated overhead; $440,000 is the pre-tax figure; $142,500 applies (1 − T) to revenue but not to the deductible costs.

questions.stem: A sunk cost is a cost that:
options: is spent on equipment that cannot be resold
is the benefit given up by using an asset the firm already owns
is spread over the life of the project as depreciation
has already been incurred and cannot be changed by accepting or rejecting the project
questions.explanation: A sunk cost is already paid (or committed) and will be incurred whatever the decision, so it is irrelevant. The benefit given up by using an owned asset is an opportunity cost, which is relevant.

questions.stem: In capital budgeting, the opportunity cost of using an asset the firm already owns is:
options: what the asset could be sold or rented for today, after tax
what the firm originally paid for the asset
the asset's accounting book value on the balance sheet
zero, because no cash leaves the firm when an owned asset is used
questions.explanation: The firm gives up the best alternative use of the asset, measured at today's market value after tax. The original price is sunk and the book value is an accounting number.

questions.stem: Ridgeline Brewing paid a consultant $85,000 last month, non-refundable, for a market study of a proposed taproom. In the taproom's cash-flow analysis the fee is a:
options: year-0 cash outflow of $85,000
sunk cost, counted at zero
capital expenditure eligible for CCA
financing cost excluded only for tax reasons
questions.explanation: The fee is already paid and cannot be recovered whether or not the taproom proceeds, so it is a sunk cost and is counted at zero.

questions.stem: Foothills Dental owns an empty unit that it could lease for $4,000 a month. A new sterilization lab would use that unit. The rent forgone is a(n):
options: sunk cost, counted at zero
financing cost, excluded
opportunity cost, counted after tax
allocated cost, counted at zero
questions.explanation: By using the unit the firm gives up rent, so the after-tax rent is an incremental cost of the project even though no cash leaves the firm.

questions.stem: A division is charged $30,000 a year by head office for utilities and administration. The charge would be the same whether or not the division launches a new product. For the new product the charge is a(n):
options: opportunity cost, counted after tax
financing cost, excluded because of debt
erosion, subtracted from revenue
allocated cost, counted at zero
questions.explanation: An allocated cost is overhead that does not change with the decision, so the incremental cost is zero.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts a sunk cost with an opportunity cost?
options: A sunk cost is already paid and excluded; an opportunity cost is a benefit given up and is included at today's value
A sunk cost is included at its historical cost; an opportunity cost is excluded because no cash is paid
Both are excluded because neither involves a cash payment to an outside party in the year
Both are included, a sunk cost at its book value and an opportunity cost at its market value today
questions.explanation: The difference is whether the decision can still change the cash flow. Sunk costs cannot be changed; opportunity costs arise only if the project is taken.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the year-0 outflow for a new plant built on land the firm already owns?
options: The construction cost of the plant
The price paid for the land six years ago
Today's after-tax market value of the land
Site-preparation cost incurred only if the project goes ahead
questions.explanation: The old purchase price is a sunk cost. What matters is today's value of the land, which is given up if the project uses it.

questions.stem: Why is the price paid for land years ago irrelevant to whether the land should be used in a project?
options: Land is never depreciated, so its original cost can never affect the firm's taxes
The historical cost of land is always lower than its market value, so it is ignored
It cannot be changed by today's decision; the cost given up is the land's sale value now
Accounting standards prohibit the use of historical cost in any forecast of cash flows
questions.explanation: The only relevant question is what the firm gives up by using the land today, namely its current after-tax market value. The old price is sunk.

questions.stem: A manager on a $70,000 salary (unchanged whether or not the project proceeds) will spend half her time on the project, and accounting allocates $35,000 a year to it. What should the analyst do?
options: Include $35,000 after tax, that is at (1 − T)
Include $35,000 before tax because salaries are not deductible
Include $70,000 because her full pay is committed
Exclude the $35,000: it is an allocated cost that does not change with the decision
questions.explanation: Her pay is the same with or without the project, so the incremental cost is zero. Allocated costs are in the 'not counted' category.

questions.stem: A consulting fee already paid to study a project must be deducted from the project's NPV if the project is accepted.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. The fee is sunk: it has been paid and cannot be changed by accepting or rejecting the project, so it is excluded.

questions.stem: If a project uses a machine the firm already owns, the cost charged to the project is the machine's current market value (after tax), not its original price.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The opportunity cost is what the firm gives up today, which is the value it could realize now; the original price is sunk.

questions.stem: A project is rejected with NPV = −$20,000. The calculation includes $50,000 (present value, after tax) for a study fee that was paid before the analysis began. What is the right interpretation?
options: Excluding the sunk fee gives NPV = +$30,000, so the project should be accepted
The fee is relevant, so the rejection stands
Excluding the fee gives NPV = −$70,000, so the rejection is even clearer
NPV cannot change, because sunk costs are part of the initial investment
questions.explanation: The study fee is sunk and must be removed: −20,000 + 50,000 = +$30,000. The wrong inclusion turned an acceptable project into a rejection.

questions.stem: Marlow Aggregates is considering a gravel plant on land it bought nine years ago for $2.8 million; the land could be sold today for $3.4 million (assume the sale triggers no tax). The plant costs $12.6 million and site preparation is $0.65 million. A $0.2 million environmental assessment was paid last year. What is the relevant year-0 cash flow?

steps.label: Opportunity cost of the land (today's value)
Year-0 cash flow = −(land + plant + site preparation)

solution: Land: charge today's value $3,400,000, not the $2,800,000 paid long ago.

errors.label: Included the sunk assessment
errors.explain: The assessment was paid last year and cannot be changed by the decision.

errors.label: Charged the original land price
errors.explain: The opportunity cost is what the land is worth today, not what was paid for it.

errors.label: Treated the owned land as free
errors.explain: Owned land is not free: the firm gives up its sale value.

questions.explanation: Year 0 includes the plant, the site preparation and the land at its current market value; the assessment is sunk.

questions.stem: Sterling Foods owns land bought for $1,000,000 that is now worth $1,600,000. Land is not depreciable. If it were sold, 50% of the capital gain would be taxable at 30%. A proposed warehouse would use this land. What opportunity cost belongs in the project's year-0 cash flow?

errors.label: Used the pre-tax market value
errors.explain: The firm would only receive the after-tax proceeds if it sold, so that is the amount given up.

errors.label: Taxed the whole capital gain
errors.explain: Only 50% of a capital gain is taxable.

errors.label: Used the original price
errors.explain: The original price is sunk; the opportunity cost is today's after-tax value.

questions.explanation: The opportunity cost of land is the after-tax cash the firm would get from selling it now: market value less tax on half of the gain.

questions.stem: Westmount Clinic owns space it could lease for $60,000 a year (pre-tax) for the next 6 years. A project will use the space. The tax rate is 35% and the discount rate is 10%. What is the present value of the after-tax opportunity cost of the rent forgone?
solution: Rent is income, so the forgone rent after tax = 60,000 × (1 − 0.35) = 39,000 a year.
keystrokes: 6 N, 10 I/Y, 39000 PMT, 0 FV, CPT PV = −169,855.17 (ignore the sign)

errors.label: Used the pre-tax rent
errors.explain: The rent forgone is taxable income, so only 65% of it is given up after tax.

errors.label: Used a 5-year annuity
errors.explain: The space is unavailable for 6 years, so N = 6.

errors.label: Added the six rents without discounting
errors.explain: Rents received in the future must be discounted at 10%.

questions.explanation: An opportunity cost can be a stream: the after-tax rent forgone each year, valued as an annuity.

questions.stem: A new line would cost $750,000 for equipment and would use a lot the firm bought five years ago for $400,000; the lot could be sold today for $520,000 (after tax). A $45,000 design fee was paid last month. What is the relevant year-0 outlay?
questions.explanation: Relevant outlay = equipment 750,000 + land at today's after-tax value 520,000 = $1,270,000. $1,315,000 adds the sunk design fee; $1,150,000 charges the lot's old price; $750,000 treats the owned lot as free.

questions.stem: A junior analyst reports an NPV of +$25,000. It subtracts a $30,000 market study already paid and ignores that the project would use a machine the firm owns, which could be sold for $90,000 after tax. What is the corrected NPV?
questions.explanation: Corrected NPV = 25,000 + 30,000 (remove the sunk study) − 90,000 (charge the opportunity cost) = −$35,000, so reject. $55,000 removes only the sunk cost; $145,000 adds the opportunity cost instead of subtracting it; −$95,000 subtracts the sunk cost a second time.

questions.stem: In capital budgeting, erosion is:
options: the decline in a project's equipment value due to wear and obsolescence
the loss in value of inventory and receivables as the project ages
a tax deduction for the cost of capital assets used up each year
a loss of cash flow on the firm's existing products caused by launching the new project
questions.explanation: Erosion (also called cannibalization) is cash flow the new product takes away from the firm's existing products. Wear of equipment is depreciation, not erosion.

questions.stem: A positive side effect (spillover or synergy) of a project is an incremental cash flow that:
options: arises on the firm's other products because of the project and is added to the project
is ignored because the project itself did not directly produce the cash flow
is counted only if the firm has guaranteed it in a signed contract
is financed with debt and is therefore treated as a financing flow
questions.explanation: Spillovers change the firm's cash flow because the project is accepted, so they belong in the analysis, after tax.

questions.stem: Lakeside Coffee launches a premium cold brew. Analysts estimate that 15% of its buyers would otherwise have bought Lakeside's regular iced coffee. The lost iced-coffee profit is an example of:
options: a sunk cost
erosion
the opportunity cost of an owned asset
a financing cost
questions.explanation: Profit lost on an existing product because of the new product is erosion and is subtracted (after tax) from the new product's cash flows.

questions.stem: A printer maker introduces a cheap new printer, and its sales of ink cartridges (a different product line) rise as a result. For the printer project, the extra ink profit is:
options: erosion that should be subtracted
a sunk cost that should be ignored
a positive side effect that should be added to the project
a financing effect that is excluded from cash flows
questions.explanation: The extra ink profit changes the firm's cash flow because the printer is launched, so it is an incremental spillover and is added after tax.

questions.stem: How does erosion differ from an opportunity cost?
options: Erosion is stated before tax in the analysis, while an opportunity cost is stated after tax
Erosion is a financing cost excluded from the analysis, while an opportunity cost is an operating cost
They are the same idea: both are costs that the firm has already incurred before the decision
Erosion is lost cash flow on other products; an opportunity cost is the value of an owned asset's best alternative use
questions.explanation: Both are incremental and both are after tax, but erosion arises on other product lines while an opportunity cost arises from using an owned asset.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT included in a project's incremental cash flows?
options: Interest paid on the bank loan raised for the project
Profit lost on an existing product that the project displaces
Extra profit on a complementary product caused by the project
Working capital the project requires
questions.explanation: Financing costs such as interest, dividends and principal repaid are never part of project cash flows. The other three change the firm's operating cash flow.

questions.stem: Why are interest payments left out of a project's cash flows?
options: Interest is not tax deductible, so it would only distort the after-tax flows
Financing is analyzed separately; the discount rate already charges for debt and equity, so interest would double count
Interest is a sunk cost that the firm pays whatever it decides about the project
Interest is always so small relative to operating cash flow that it can be ignored
questions.explanation: The project's cash flows are discounted at a rate that already reflects the cost of funds. Subtracting interest as well would charge for financing twice.

questions.stem: Zenith Bikes expects a rival to launch an equivalent e-bike next year whether or not Zenith does, so Zenith's older model will lose those sales anyway. How should the lost sales be treated in the e-bike analysis?
options: Deduct them in full, because any decline in existing sales counts
Deduct half of them, because the loss is partly caused by the project
Ignore them: erosion is relevant only when the sales would not otherwise be lost
Add them as a sunk cost
questions.explanation: With or without the e-bike, the older model loses those sales, so the project does not change the firm's cash flow there. Erosion is relevant only if the sales would not be lost anyway.

questions.stem: Interest on the loan used to fund a project is deducted when computing the project's incremental cash flows.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Interest is a financing cost: it is part of the cash flow to creditors, not of the cash flow from the project's assets. The discount rate accounts for it.

questions.stem: A project's NPV is +$12,000 when financing is left to the discount rate. An analyst who also subtracts the loan's after-tax interest from the cash flows reports −$30,000. Which interpretation is right?
options: The −$30,000 is more conservative because it deducts interest, and is therefore correct
Both are correct; the sign depends on how the lender structures the loan
Only the −$30,000 captures the tax shield on interest, so it is the better figure
The −$30,000 double counts the cost of debt; the +$12,000 figure is the correct one
questions.explanation: The discount rate already charges for the cost of capital, so removing interest from the cash flows and discounting gives the right NPV. Subtracting interest as well counts the cost of funds twice.

questions.stem: A negative impact on the cash flows of an existing product from introducing a new product is called _____.
options: erosion
synergy
depreciation
recapture
questions.explanation: Erosion is the effect of a new product on the cash flows of the firm's existing products.

questions.stem: A project should always deduct the profit it takes from existing products, even if a competitor would have taken those sales anyway.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Erosion is relevant only when the sales would not otherwise be lost; if they would be lost anyway, the project does not change the cash flow.

questions.stem: Sunridge's new snack takes sales from an existing snack, costing $85,000 a year of pre-tax profit. The tax rate is 30%. What is the annual after-tax cash-flow effect of this erosion?
questions.explanation: Lost profit is a pre-tax loss, so the after-tax effect is −85,000(1 − 0.30) = −$59,500. −$85,000 leaves it before tax; −$25,500 multiplies by T instead of (1 − T); $59,500 has the wrong sign (erosion lowers cash flow).

questions.stem: Which pairing of cash-flow type and tax multiplier is correct?
options: Revenues and expenses: both multiplied by T
Cash expenses and revenues: counted in full (× 1)
Capital expenditure and the change in NWC: counted in full (× 1)
CCA and sunk costs: multiplied by (1 − T)
questions.explanation: CAPEX and NWC are cash moved through the balance sheet, counted at 100%. Revenues and cash expenses are × (1 − T) and CCA is × T.

questions.stem: Which cash flows are multiplied by (1 − T) to find their after-tax effect?
options: Sunk costs and allocated costs
CAPEX and changes in NWC
CCA only
Revenues and cash expenses
questions.explanation: Each $1 of revenue attracts $T of tax, leaving (1 − T); each $1 of deductible expense saves $T of tax, so it costs (1 − T).

questions.stem: A $20,000 delivery truck bought for a project falls into which category of cash flow?
options: Counted in full (× 1): capital expenditure
× (1 − T): an expense
× T: a tax shield
× 0: a sunk cost
questions.explanation: The purchase price is cash paid out of after-tax funds with no immediate tax effect, so it is counted at 100%. The tax relief arrives later as CCA.

questions.stem: The tax cash flows from selling a depreciated machine (recapture, terminal loss or capital gain) belong to which category?
options: Revenue-type flows, multiplied by (1 − T)
Other tax flows, handled by the CF_AT formula
Tax shields, like CCA, multiplied by T
Capital expenditure, counted in full (× 1)
questions.explanation: The fifth category is salvage with tax effects. It does not reduce to a simple multiplier; the sheet formula CF_AT = POD − T[min(ACB, POD) − UCC] − 0.5T max(POD − ACB, 0) is used.

questions.stem: Why is a $10,000 increase in cash expenses multiplied by (1 − T) while $10,000 of CCA is multiplied by T?
options: Expenses are subject to tax, but CCA is exempt from tax, so the multiplier reverses
CCA is usually much smaller than cash expenses, so it is scaled down by T
The expense is cash paid, partly offset by tax saved; CCA involves no cash, so only the tax saved counts
Both are multiplied by T, but CCA is reported on a separate line of the income statement
questions.explanation: A cash expense of $1 costs $1 but saves $T of tax, net (1 − T). CCA costs nothing in cash but still saves $T of tax, net T.

questions.stem: Which of these items is NOT counted at 100% (× 1) in the analysis?
options: Capital expenditure
An increase in net working capital
Recovery of net working capital at the end
Revenue
questions.explanation: Revenue is taxed, so it is × (1 − T). CAPEX, ΔNWC and the NWC recovery are counted in full.

questions.stem: Why is capital expenditure counted at 100% rather than at (1 − T)?
options: It is cash paid from already-taxed funds with no immediate tax effect; tax relief comes later through CCA
Capital assets are exempt from tax, so no multiplier applies to their cost
CAPEX is a sunk cost, since the money is committed once the project is approved
The tax saving is received immediately as a full deduction in the year of purchase
questions.explanation: The purchase price itself is not an expense, so it does not reduce tax when it is paid. It reduces tax gradually through CCA.

questions.stem: At T = 30%, which ordering shows the after-tax value of $1 of each item from smallest to largest?
options: Sunk cost ($0) < revenue ($0.70) < CCA ($0.30) < CAPEX ($1.00)
Sunk cost ($0) < CCA ($0.30) < revenue ($0.70) < CAPEX ($1.00)
CCA ($0.30) < sunk cost ($0) < CAPEX ($1.00) < revenue ($0.70)
Sunk cost ($0) < CAPEX ($1.00) < CCA ($0.30) < revenue ($0.70)
questions.explanation: Multipliers: sunk × 0, CCA × T = 0.30, revenue × (1 − T) = 0.70, CAPEX × 1.

questions.stem: A dollar of additional revenue adds $(1 − T) to after-tax cash flow.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. The firm pays $T of tax on each extra dollar of revenue and keeps $(1 − T).

questions.stem: CCA is a cash flow that is multiplied by (1 − T).
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. CCA is a non-cash deduction; its cash effect is the tax it saves, so it is multiplied by T.

questions.stem: Revenues and cash expenses are multiplied by _____ to get their after-tax effect.
options: T
questions.explanation: Each dollar of revenue or deductible expense changes tax by T, leaving (1 − T) of the pre-tax amount.

questions.stem: With T = 30%, what is the cash effect of $1 of CCA?
options: +$0.70: a tax saving
−$0.30: a tax payment
$0: CCA is non-cash
+$0.30: a tax saving
questions.explanation: CCA reduces taxable income by $1, which saves $0.30 of tax. It is a non-cash deduction but not a zero-cash item.

questions.stem: For each of the following, determine the after-tax cash flow, assuming the tax rate is 30%: (a) an increase in sales revenue of $100,000.
solution: Revenue is category (c): multiply by (1 − T).

errors.label: Left the revenue before tax
errors.explain: Extra revenue is taxed; only (1 − T) of it is kept.

errors.label: Multiplied by T instead of (1 − T)
errors.explain: T is the tax paid; the after-tax amount is (1 − T).

questions.explanation: Revenue is multiplied by (1 − T): $100,000 × 0.70 = $70,000.

questions.stem: For each of the following, determine the after-tax cash flow, assuming the tax rate is 30%: (b) $150,000 spent last year on advertising the benefits of this project.
solution: The advertising was spent last year and cannot be changed by the decision: it is a sunk cost.
Sunk costs are multiplied by 0: after-tax cash flow = $0

errors.label: Treated the advertising as a cost after tax
errors.explain: A sunk cost is not incremental, whatever its tax treatment.

errors.label: Treated the advertising as a pre-tax outflow
errors.explain: The money was spent last year; it is not changed by the decision.

questions.explanation: Sunk costs belong to category (a) and count at zero.

questions.stem: For each of the following, determine the after-tax cash flow, assuming the tax rate is 30%: (c) selling an asset for $197,000 which you had bought for $590,000 and had depreciated for tax purposes to an undeducted capital cost of $155,566.41.

steps.label: CF_AT = POD − T × recapture − 0.5 × T × gain

solution: POD is below ACB, so there is no capital gain: max(197,000 − 590,000, 0) = 0

errors.label: Taxed the whole proceeds
errors.explain: Only the excess over UCC is recaptured, not the whole sale price.

errors.label: Used ACB instead of min(ACB, POD) in the recapture
errors.explain: The sale price is below cost, so recapture cannot exceed POD − UCC.

errors.label: Used POD − ACB as the tax base
errors.explain: POD − ACB is negative here, which wrongly creates a tax refund.

errors.label: Ignored tax on the sale
errors.explain: The recapture of CCA is taxable income and must be taxed.

questions.explanation: The asset sold below its cost, so there is no capital gain; the only tax is on the recapture of CCA (POD − UCC).

questions.stem: This year, Mid-Prairie Dairy's cheese project has revenue of $420,000, labour of $150,000, materials of $95,000 and CCA of $28,000. It also buys $200,000 of equipment and adds $18,000 to working capital this year, and a $25,000 study was paid earlier. The tax rate is 30%. What is the project's net after-tax cash flow for this year?

steps.label: Revenue less cash expenses, after tax (× (1 − T))

solution: CAPEX and NWC counted in full: −200,000 − 18,000 = −218,000

errors.label: Deducted the sunk study
errors.explain: A study paid earlier is sunk and counts at zero.

errors.label: Multiplied CAPEX by (1 − T)
errors.explain: Capital expenditure is counted in full; its tax relief comes through CCA.

errors.label: Multiplied the NWC change by (1 − T)
errors.explain: Changes in working capital are counted in full.

errors.label: Left out the CCA tax shield
errors.explain: CCA saves T × 28,000 of tax even though it is non-cash.

questions.explanation: Run each item through its category: expenses and revenue at (1 − T), CCA at T, CAPEX and NWC at 1, the sunk study at 0.

questions.stem: A project raises annual cash expenses by $64,000. The tax rate is 35%. What is the after-tax cash-flow effect each year?
questions.explanation: A deductible expense costs (1 − T) of its amount: −64,000(1 − 0.35) = −$41,600. −$64,000 ignores the tax saving; −$22,400 multiplies by T instead of (1 − T); $41,600 has the wrong sign.

questions.stem: In a year the firm claims $36,000 of CCA on a project asset. The tax rate is 30%. What is the cash effect of the CCA that year?
questions.explanation: CCA is non-cash, but it saves T × CCA of tax: 0.30 × 36,000 = $10,800. $36,000 counts the CCA itself as a cash inflow; $25,200 multiplies by (1 − T); $0 treats non-cash as no effect at all.

questions.stem: Gordon Gears' project has year-1 revenue of $200,000 and cash costs of $120,000. A $25,000 study was paid last year. The tax rate is 30%; ignore CCA and capital spending. What is the year-1 after-tax operating cash flow?
questions.explanation: Operating flow = (200,000 − 120,000)(1 − 0.30) = $56,000. $38,500 subtracts the sunk study; $80,000 is before tax; $20,000 taxes the revenue but not the deductible costs.

questions.stem: Operating cash flow (OCF) for a project year is:
options: net income minus depreciation
EBIT − taxes − capital expenditure
revenue minus total expenses including CCA
EBIT + depreciation (CCA) − taxes
questions.explanation: OCF = EBIT + D − Tax: start from EBIT, add back the non-cash CCA and subtract the tax actually paid. Net income minus depreciation moves the wrong way; capital expenditure belongs to free cash flow, not OCF.

questions.stem: Which expression equals OCF, where S is sales, C is cash costs, D is CCA and T is the tax rate?
questions.explanation: After-tax operating profit is (S − C)(1 − T), and CCA adds a tax shield of T × D. The last option is net income, which omits the add-back of D.

questions.stem: An analyst computes OCF as net income plus CCA. This is the:
options: top-down approach
bottom-up approach
tax-shield approach
free-cash-flow approach
questions.explanation: Bottom-up starts from net income and adds back depreciation. Top-down is S − C − Tax; the tax-shield approach is (S − C)(1 − T) + T × D.

questions.stem: An analyst writes OCF = (S − C)(1 − T) + T × D. This is called the:
options: bottom-up approach
top-down approach
tax-shield approach
stand-alone approach
questions.explanation: The T × D term is the depreciation (CCA) tax shield, so this form is the tax-shield approach. All four forms give the same OCF.

questions.stem: How does a project's OCF differ from its free cash flow in the same year?
options: FCF is OCF with the tax shield removed
FCF is OCF with interest added back
FCF includes CCA but OCF does not
FCF is OCF less CAPEX and the increase in NWC
questions.explanation: OCF is the cash generated by operations. Free cash flow also subtracts the cash invested in assets (CAPEX) and in working capital: FCF = OCF − CAPEX − ΔNWC.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT enter a project's operating cash flow?
options: Interest paid on the project's financing
Sales revenue
Cash operating expenses
Income tax on EBIT
questions.explanation: Interest is a financing cost and never appears in project cash flows. Revenue, cash expenses and the tax on EBIT are all part of OCF.

questions.stem: Why is depreciation (CCA) added back when OCF is computed from EBIT?
options: It is a tax payment that must be reversed to find cash
It is non-cash: it reduced EBIT but no cash left the firm
It is financed with debt, so its cash cost is already counted
It measures the fall in the asset's market value
questions.explanation: CCA is subtracted to find taxable income, so EBIT is understated relative to cash. Adding it back recovers the cash, and the lower tax it caused is already in the Tax term.

questions.stem: Holding sales, costs and the tax rate (30%) fixed, CCA rises by $10,000. What happens to OCF?
options: It rises by $10,000
It falls by $7,000
It rises by $3,000, because taxes fall by that amount
It is unchanged, because CCA is non-cash
questions.explanation: In OCF = (S − C)(1 − T) + T × D, only the T × D term changes: 0.30 × 10,000 = $3,000. The extra CCA is non-cash but lowers the tax bill.

questions.stem: Interest expense is subtracted when computing a project's operating cash flow.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Interest is a financing cost; it is excluded from project OCF and the discount rate carries the cost of capital.

questions.stem: Starting from the same sales, costs, CCA and tax rate, the bottom-up form (NI + D) and the tax-shield form can give different OCF values.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. All the forms are algebraically identical: NI + D = (S − C − D)(1 − T) + D = (S − C)(1 − T) + T × D.

questions.stem: OCF = (S − C)(1 − T) + T × _____ , where the missing term is the CCA claimed.
options: I0
ΔNWC
interest
D
questions.explanation: The tax shield on CCA is T × D, where D is the CCA (depreciation) claimed in the year.

questions.stem: A problem gives EBIT, the CCA claimed and the tax paid for the year. Which formula gives OCF directly?
