questions.stem: Foothills Implements will build a new plant on land it bought years ago for $90,000 and that could be sold today for $150,000 after tax. Which amount belongs in the year-0 cash flow of the expansion project?
options: $150,000, the after-tax value of the land if it were sold today
$90,000, the price originally paid for the land
$0, because the firm already owns the land
$60,000, the gain on the land since it was bought
questions.explanation: The relevant cost of using land is what the firm gives up by not selling it: its current after-tax market value, which is an opportunity cost. The original price is sunk, and owning the land does not make it free.

questions.stem: A new line of lightweight balers will cost the firm $40,000 of contribution margin a year on its existing heavyweight line. How does this erosion enter the expansion project's cash flows?
options: It is ignored because the heavyweight line is a separate product
As a one-time cost at time 0 of $40,000
As a lost after-tax cash flow, $40,000 x (1 - T) every year, subtracted from the project
As a gain, because the lost sales are replaced by new sales
questions.explanation: Erosion is an incremental effect caused by taking the project, so it belongs in the project's cash flows. Lost revenue is taxed like revenue, so it reduces cash flow by 40,000 x (1 - T) in each year it lasts.

questions.stem: In an expansion project, the net working capital invested at time 0 is recovered at the _____ of the project.
options: start
midpoint
end
end of year 1
questions.explanation: NWC is tied up while the project operates and is released when the project ends, so the recovery appears as a positive cash flow in the last year. It is not taxed because it is a return of capital already counted at 100%.

questions.stem: How do the cash flows of an expansion project differ from those of a replacement project?
options: An expansion uses the project's own flows; a replacement uses the differences between the new and the old equipment (net acquisition cost, net salvage, incremental savings)
An expansion is taxed at the full rate; a replacement is taxed at half the rate
An expansion ignores CCA; a replacement includes CCA
An expansion is discounted at the cost of capital; a replacement is discounted at the cost of the old machine
questions.explanation: Both use the same NPV machinery, but a replacement is evaluated incrementally: sell the old, buy the new, and count only what changes. An expansion adds a stand-alone set of flows.

questions.stem: Which of the following should NOT be included in the cash flows of an expansion project?
options: The after-tax value of land the project will use
The initial investment in working capital
The after-tax revenue lost on an existing product
The $25,000 feasibility study that has already been paid
questions.explanation: The feasibility study is a sunk cost: it has been spent whether or not the project goes ahead, so its incremental cash flow is zero. The land, working capital and erosion are all caused by the decision to go ahead.

questions.stem: Why does the NPV of an expansion add the PV of the CCA tax shield as a separate item rather than including CCA in the annual operating cash flow?
options: CCA is a cash outflow that must be discounted at a higher rate
CCA is not a cash flow; its only value is the tax it saves, which the PV formula captures once for the whole declining-balance schedule
CCA is already included in revenue, so it would be double counted
Because CCA is the only item taxed at the rate T rather than (1 - T)
questions.explanation: The operating cash flow (S - C)(1 - T) deliberately leaves CCA out. The shield T x CCA is a separate stream of declining flows, valued by the formula I0 d T/(k + d) x first-year factor, less the salvage term. Counting CCA in both places would double count.

questions.stem: An expansion project has an NPV of -$31,400 at the firm's 12% cost of capital. What does this result say?
options: The project earns exactly 12% and the firm should be indifferent
The project loses $31,400 of accounting profit in year 1
The project should be accepted because its cash flows are positive after year 0
The project earns less than 12% and destroys value; reject it unless there are strategic benefits not in the cash flows
questions.explanation: NPV is the value added in today's dollars, after paying investors their required return. A negative NPV means the PV of inflows is less than the PV of outflows, so the IRR is below 12%.

questions.stem: Which items make up the time-0 cash flow of an expansion NPV?
options: Capital expenditure, sunk feasibility costs, and interest on the financing
Capital expenditure, initial net working capital, and the opportunity cost of any assets the project uses
Capital expenditure and the first year's CCA tax shield
Capital expenditure and the expected salvage value
questions.explanation: CF0 = -CAPEX - NWC0 - opportunity cost. Sunk costs and financing costs are not incremental, the CCA shield is a later-year item and salvage arrives at the end.

questions.stem: If an expansion project's equipment is not sold at the end and stays in a pool that holds other assets, the PV of the CCA tax shield has no salvage term.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The salvage term removes the shields lost when the proceeds of a sale reduce the pool. With no sale there is no reduction, so only the first term, I0 d T/(k + d) x first-year factor, remains.

questions.stem: Red Deer Welding will add a $150,000 line (CCA rate 30%, half-year rule). It earns $80,000 a year before tax for 3 years, needs $10,000 of working capital recovered at the end, and will be sold for $30,000 in year 3 (the pool stays open). A $5,000 feasibility study was already paid. T = 30%, k = 10%. What is the NPV?

NPV = $36,460.84. Counting the sunk study lowers it by $5,000; forgetting the NWC recovery, dropping the salvage term or omitting the half-year factor each give a different wrong value.

questions.stem: Saskatoon Seed Co. buys $300,000 of equipment (CCA rate 20%, half-year rule) for an expansion and sells it for $60,000 at the end of year 5; the pool stays open. T = 40% and k = 12%. What is the present value of the CCA tax shield?

questions.stem: Dunvegan Printing will buy a new press for $190,000 and sell its old press today for $45,000. What is the relevant time-0 outlay for the replacement analysis?
options: $190,000, the full price of the new press
$235,000, the new press plus the old press
$145,000, the net acquisition cost
$45,000, the amount received for the old press
questions.explanation: In a replacement only the differences count: the firm pays 190,000 and receives 45,000, so the net acquisition cost is 145,000. This net figure is also the amount that goes into the PV of CCA tax shield.

questions.stem: Bow River Dairy could sell its old pasteurizer for $8,000 in five years if it keeps it. If it replaces the machine today, the new unit will be worth $20,000 in five years. How is the salvage handled in the replacement NPV?
options: Net salvage of $12,000 (20,000 - 8,000) at year 5, because the old machine's future sale is given up
Salvage of $20,000 at year 5, because the old machine is already sold
Salvage of $28,000 at year 5, the sum of both machines
No salvage, because salvage values are not incremental
questions.explanation: Replacing now means we do not sell the old machine in year 5, so its $8,000 is forgone. The incremental salvage is the new machine's value minus the old machine's: 20,000 - 8,000 = 12,000.

questions.stem: In a replacement project the net acquisition cost equals the cost of the new machine minus the _____ of the old machine today.
options: UCC
resale value
original cost
salvage value in five years
questions.explanation: The cash the firm gets by selling the old machine now reduces the net outlay. The old machine's UCC and original cost are accounting history; they only matter through tax, and in an open pool the sale has no immediate tax effect.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts net acquisition cost with net salvage value in a replacement NPV?
options: Net acquisition cost is taxed at (1 - T); net salvage is taxed at T
Net acquisition cost uses the old machine's UCC; net salvage uses its ACB
Both occur at time 0 but net salvage is discounted for the old machine's remaining life
Net acquisition cost is a time-0 flow (new cost minus old resale today); net salvage is a time-N flow (new salvage minus the old machine's salvage forgone)
questions.explanation: Each is a difference between new and old, but they occur at different dates: the acquisition difference now and the salvage difference at the end of the horizon. Both then feed the PV of CCA tax shield formula.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a relevant cash flow when deciding whether to replace an old machine?
options: The price paid for the old machine five years ago
The resale value of the old machine today
The after-tax cost savings from the new machine
The salvage value the old machine would fetch if kept
questions.explanation: The old machine's original price is a sunk cost; nothing the firm decides now can change it. The resale value today, the extra savings and the forgone future salvage are all caused by the replacement decision.

questions.stem: Why is the old machine's future salvage subtracted from the new machine's salvage in the replacement NPV?
options: Because old equipment is always worth less than new equipment
Because salvage is a tax expense that offsets the CCA shield
Selling the old machine now means the firm will not receive its future salvage, so that cash flow is lost
Because net salvage is always negative in a replacement
questions.explanation: Incremental analysis compares the world with replacement to the world without. Without replacement the firm sells the old machine at N; with replacement it sells the new one. The difference S_new - S_old is the incremental cash flow.

questions.stem: A replacement project has NPV = +$47,867 at the firm's required return. What does this mean?
options: The new machine will earn $47,867 of accounting profit in its first year
The old machine is worth $47,867 more than the new one
Replacing the old machine now adds $47,867 of value in today's dollars compared with keeping it
The firm saves exactly $47,867 a year over the life of the new machine
questions.explanation: Replacement NPV is the PV of the incremental flows. A positive value means the savings, salvage differences and CCA shield outweigh the net outlay, so replace.

questions.stem: Maple Ridge Moulding replaces a machine with UCC of $63,000 by a new one in the same CCA class. The old machine is sold for $60,000, and other assets stay in the class. What tax effect does the $3,000 shortfall have at the sale?
options: None at the sale: the pool stays open, and the net acquisition (new cost minus $60,000) goes into the PV of CCA shield
A $3,000 terminal loss saves 3,000 x T of tax now
A $3,000 capital loss, half deductible
A $3,000 recapture, taxed at the full rate
questions.explanation: Because the class stays open, the sale just reduces the pool's UCC by the proceeds. The seminar's treatment uses the net acquisition cost in the CCA formula and ignores any immediate recapture or terminal loss.

questions.stem: In a replacement NPV, which investment amount multiplies d x T/(k + d) in the PV of CCA tax shield?
options: The full purchase price of the new machine
The old machine's UCC
The new machine's cost plus the old machine's resale value
The net acquisition cost: new cost minus old resale today
questions.explanation: The sale of the old machine reduces the pool, so only the net addition to the pool generates new shields. The seminar uses 220,000 = 280,000 - 60,000 in its worked example.

questions.stem: A new machine will raise annual sales by $85,000 compared with the old machine. How is this revenue treated in the replacement NPV?
options: The full revenue of the new machine is counted, after tax
Only the increase of $85,000 is counted, after tax at (1 - T)
It is counted before tax, because replacement revenue is not taxed
It is ignored, because the old machine already produced the base revenue
questions.explanation: Replacement is evaluated incrementally. The relevant revenue is the difference between what the firm earns with the new machine and what it would earn with the old one, and that difference is taxed like any revenue.

questions.stem: Foothills Moulding will replace a machine. New cost $120,000; old machine sells for $40,000 now and for $6,000 in 5 years; the new one sells for $15,000 in 5 years. The new machine saves $41,000 a year before tax for 5 years. CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, pool open. T = 35%, k = 10%. What is the NPV of replacing?
questions.explanation: Net acquisition = 80,000; net salvage = 9,000; after-tax savings = 26,650 a year (PV 101,024.47); PV of net salvage = 5,588.29; PV of CCA = 16,514.25. NPV = -80,000 + 101,024.47 + 5,588.29 + 16,514.25 = $43,127.01. Using gross figures, leaving out the CCA shield, or using the new machine's salvage instead of the net salvage each give one of the other values.

questions.stem: Cascade Fabricators replaces a machine in a class with CCA rate 25%. New cost $260,000; old resale today $55,000; salvage in 4 years $20,000 (new) and $9,000 (old). AII applies, T = 40%, k = 10%. What is the present value of the CCA tax shield on the replacement?

PV = $59,087.15. Using gross figures (260,000 and 20,000), leaving out the salvage term, using the half-year rule or flipping the sign of the salvage term each gives a different value.

questions.stem: Fraser Bakery is considering a new oven that earns no extra revenue but cuts energy and labour costs by $36,000 a year before tax. What kind of project is this?
options: An expansion project, whose benefit is new revenue
A replacement project with no relevant tax effect
A bid-price problem, whose benefit is the contract price
A cost-cutting proposal, whose benefit is the after-tax cost saving
questions.explanation: A cost-cutting project has no new sales. Its operating benefit is the saving in costs, which raises taxable income, so the cash flow each year is saving x (1 - T), plus the CCA shield from the new equipment.

questions.stem: How do the after-tax cash flows of a cost-cutting project differ from those of an expansion project?
options: Cost savings are not taxed because no cash is received
The operating benefit is saving x (1 - T) instead of (revenue - costs) x (1 - T); the CAPEX, NWC, salvage and CCA shield are treated the same way
Cost-cutting projects are discounted at a lower rate because they are safer
Cost-cutting projects have no CCA tax shield because they add no revenue
questions.explanation: A dollar saved in costs raises pre-tax income by a dollar just like a dollar of new revenue, so it is taxed at T. The equipment still qualifies for CCA, so the shield stays.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT part of the NPV of a cost-cutting investment?
options: The after-tax annual saving
The extra inventory (NWC) the project requires, recovered at the end
Revenue from additional sales
The PV of the CCA tax shield on the new equipment
questions.explanation: By definition a cost-cutting project does not change sales. Its benefits are lower costs, plus the usual items: CAPEX, NWC, salvage and the CCA shield.

questions.stem: Why is a $50,000 annual cost saving multiplied by (1 - T) when evaluating the project?
options: Lower costs raise taxable income, so the firm pays tax on the saving and keeps only (1 - T) of it
Because the saving is a non-cash item that only appears on the income statement
Because cost savings are a capital expenditure
Because the tax rate on savings is always the capital gains rate
questions.explanation: Expenses are deductible, so reducing them leaves less to deduct. The extra taxable income costs T per dollar saved, and the net benefit is saving x (1 - T).

questions.stem: A cost-cutting analysis finds that the required pre-tax saving for NPV = 0 is $110,211 a year, and engineers forecast savings of $95,000. What should the firm conclude?
options: Accept: the forecast saving is large enough to cover the cost of the equipment
Reject: forecast savings are below the break-even level, so the NPV is negative
Accept: any positive saving makes the NPV positive
The project breaks even because savings are 86% of the requirement
questions.explanation: The required saving is the level at which the NPV is exactly zero. Forecasts below it give a negative NPV; forecasts above it give a positive NPV. The 86% is irrelevant because NPV is linear in the saving, not proportional.

questions.stem: To find the pre-tax annual saving that makes a cost-cutting project break even, which sequence is correct?
options: Divide the equipment cost by the number of years, then multiply by (1 - T)
Divide the equipment cost by the annuity factor, then multiply by (1 - T)
Set NPV = 0, solve for the PV of savings, divide by N, then divide by T
Set NPV = 0, solve for the PV of after-tax savings, divide by the annuity factor, then divide by (1 - T)
questions.explanation: With CF0, salvage and the CCA shield known, the PV of the after-tax savings must make up the rest. Dividing by the annuity factor gives the after-tax annual saving; dividing by (1 - T) un-taxes it.

questions.stem: In a cost-cutting NPV, the CCA tax shield is valued only on the cost of the new equipment, not on the cost savings.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The shield arises from deductions for depreciating the asset: CCA x T. Cost savings are an operating item taxed at (1 - T) and carry no shield of their own.

questions.stem: A cost-cutting machine requires a $15,000 increase in inventory that is released when the machine is retired. How is this treated?
options: As a $15,000 outflow at time 0 and a $15,000 inflow at the end, neither taxed
As a tax-deductible expense in year 1
As a $15,000 reduction of the CCA base
As an outflow at time 0 only, because inventory is sold during the project
questions.explanation: NWC is counted at 100% when it is invested and again when it is recovered. It does not enter the CCA calculation, and it is not taxed.

questions.stem: Okotoks Bottling is buying a $120,000 filler (CCA rate 20%, half-year rule) that saves $38,000 a year before tax for 4 years. It needs $8,000 more inventory, recovered at the end, and sells for $20,000 in year 4 (pool open). T = 35%, k = 9%. What is the NPV?
questions.explanation: CF0 = -128,000. After-tax saving = 38,000 x 0.65 = 24,700 (PV 80,021.08). Year-4 salvage + NWC = 28,000 (PV 19,835.91). PV CCA = 24,349.71. NPV = -$3,793.30, so reject. Leaving savings untaxed makes the NPV look positive.

questions.stem: Saskatoon Metalworks can buy a $250,000 machine (CCA rate 30%, half-year rule, salvage $35,000 at year 4, pool open) that cuts costs for 4 years. T = 30% and k = 12%. What annual pre-tax saving makes the NPV exactly zero?

questions.stem: Foothills Machining must submit a fixed price per unit for a five-year supply contract. It wants the lowest price that still earns its required return on the investment. What is this problem called, and what is the benchmark?
options: A bid-price problem: choose the price that makes accounting profit equal to zero
An equivalent annual cost problem: choose the price that equals the EAC
A bid-price problem: choose the price that makes the project's NPV equal to zero
A sensitivity analysis: choose the price that is 10% above cost
questions.explanation: At the bid price the project earns exactly the required return, so NPV = 0. Any lower price loses value (the winner's curse); any higher price risks losing the contract.

questions.stem: In a bid-price calculation, the minimum acceptable price is the one that sets the project's NPV equal to _____.
options: the CCA tax shield
the initial investment
zero
the profit margin
questions.explanation: NPV = 0 means the project earns exactly the discount rate: it covers all costs and pays investors their required return. That is the lowest price the firm can charge without destroying value.

questions.stem: How does the bid price based on NPV = 0 differ from the price at which accounting profit is zero?
options: The NPV price also covers the investors' required return on the capital tied up, so it is higher
The accounting price is higher because it includes depreciation
They are always identical when the tax rate is zero
The NPV price ignores the cost of equipment because it is already spent
questions.explanation: Accounting break-even only covers expenses including depreciation; it ignores the time value of money. NPV break-even makes the PV of after-tax flows equal the investment, which requires a larger annual net revenue.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a step in finding a bid price?
options: Set NPV = 0 and compute the PV of the known flows (CAPEX, NWC, salvage, CCA shield)
Divide the remaining PV by the annuity factor to get the required after-tax annual amount
Divide by (1 - T) and add the cash costs
Divide the required after-tax annuity by the number of years N
questions.explanation: A level annual amount that has a given present value is found by dividing by the annuity factor, not by N, because the payments occur in the future. The other three steps are the standard sequence.

questions.stem: Why must the required after-tax annual amount be divided by (1 - T) when finding the bid price?
options: Because the tax rate applies only to the first year
Revenue minus costs is taxed, so before-tax net revenue must be larger than the after-tax amount needed
Because (1 - T) converts a nominal flow into a real flow
Because the CCA shield must be added back
questions.explanation: The after-tax annuity equals [(P - v)Q - FC](1 - T). To recover the pre-tax figure we undo the tax by dividing by (1 - T), then add the cash costs to get total revenue.

questions.stem: Okotoks Steel bids exactly the NPV = 0 price and wins the contract. What does that imply about the project?
options: It earns a 0% return
It creates a positive NPV equal to the CCA tax shield
It breaks even on accounting profit but not on cash flow
It earns exactly its required return: IRR = k, NPV = 0, with no value added or lost
questions.explanation: At the break-even price the PV of the inflows equals the PV of the outflows at the required rate, so the IRR equals the required return. The firm is indifferent; to add value it would need a price above that level.

questions.stem: In the bid-price equation, after-tax net revenue = [(P - v)Q - FC](1 - T). Which item is NOT inside the bracket?
options: Variable cost per unit v
CCA, because its tax shield is valued separately through PV_CCA
Fixed cash costs FC
Price per unit P
questions.explanation: The bracket contains cash revenue and cash costs only. CCA is not a cash cost; its tax saving is counted once in the PV of CCA tax shield, so including it in the bracket would double count.

questions.stem: If the required return rises and nothing else changes, the bid price per unit rises.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A higher k lowers the PV of salvage and tax shields and raises the annuity needed to repay the investment at that rate; the required after-tax net revenue grows and so does the price.

questions.stem: To submit a bid, a firm must put land it owns at the project's disposal, with an after-tax market value of $300,000 now and $320,000 in five years. Which cash flows go into the bid calculation?
options: Nothing, because the firm already owns the land
-$300,000 at time 0 only
-$300,000 at time 0 and +$320,000 at year 5
The land's original purchase price
questions.explanation: Land has an opportunity cost: the project gives up the after-tax sale proceeds today, and the land comes back at its after-tax value at the end. Both flows are in the NPV = 0 equation.

questions.stem: Bow Valley Plastics will bid on a 4-year contract for 25,000 units a year. Equipment costs $620,000 (CCA rate 30%, half-year rule, sold for $70,000 at year 4, pool open). NWC of $60,000 is recovered at the end. Variable cost is $18.40 a unit, fixed cash costs $150,000 a year, T = 30%, k = 14%. What is the lowest price per unit that gives NPV = 0?

Nechako Components bids on a 5-year contract for 30,000 units a year. Equipment costs $540,000 (CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, sold for $60,000 in year 5, pool open); NWC of $45,000 is recovered at the end. Variable cost is $22.60 a unit and fixed cash costs are $210,000 a year. T = 35%, k = 12%. What is the lowest price per unit that gives NPV = 0?

What price per unit does it need?

questions.stem: Nechako Components (equipment $540,000, CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, sold for $60,000 at year 5, pool open; NWC $45,000; variable cost $22.60; fixed cash costs $210,000; T = 35%; k = 12%) can sell its product at $38.50. How many units a year must it sell for NPV = 0? Answer in units, to the nearest unit.
solution: (P - v)Q - FC = pre-tax net revenue, so Q = (pre-tax + FC)/(P - v)

questions.stem: Cascade Rail owns an old locomotive that earns nothing more. It is deciding whether to sell it at the end of year 5 or keep it and keep claiming CCA. What is the opportunity cost of selling at year 5?
options: The present value of the CCA tax shields it gives up on the remaining UCC
The original purchase price of the locomotive
The CCA already claimed in years 1 to 5
The recapture tax that would be due on the sale
questions.explanation: Selling ends the CCA stream. At year 5 that stream is worth UCC x d x T/(k + d). Past CCA is history, and recapture tax is already inside the after-tax sale proceeds.

questions.stem: Clean Air Industries owns land it could use for a new sensor line. Which three choices should it compare?
options: Build the project, sell the project, or abandon the project
Sell the land now and buy equivalent land back later; keep renting it out; use it for the new project
Sell the land, keep the land idle, or give the land away
Use the land now, use the land in a year, or use the land in two years
questions.explanation: The land has alternative uses and each is a different set of cash flows. The lecture compares the two existing uses first (sell and rebuy versus rent) and then tests the winner against the project.

questions.stem: When comparing a sale at year N with continuing to hold the asset, the sale gives up the present value of the remaining CCA _____.
options: recapture
terminal loss
capital gain
tax shield
questions.explanation: Continuing to hold keeps the declining stream of CCA deductions going. Their tax saving, T x CCA, is the shield the sale gives up, valued as a declining perpetuity.

questions.stem: How do the cash flows from selling at year N differ from the cash flows from holding the asset?
options: Selling gives the after-tax proceeds now but ends the CCA shield; holding keeps the shield and receives no proceeds now
Selling gives the CCA shield now; holding gives the proceeds
Selling is taxed; holding is not taxed
Selling and holding give the same cash flows except for timing
questions.explanation: Selling swaps a lump of after-tax cash (POD less tax on recapture or plus the terminal-loss refund) for the loss of all later CCA shields. Holding does the opposite.

questions.stem: When valuing 'sell at year 5 versus hold', which of the following should NOT enter the analysis?
options: The after-tax proceeds from the sale
The tax effect (recapture or terminal loss) of the sale
The original purchase price of the asset
The CCA tax shields that would continue if the asset is held
questions.explanation: The purchase price is a sunk cost. Only what changes between selling and holding matters: the proceeds, their tax effect and the lost future shields.

questions.stem: Why can a firm be better off selling an asset at year N even though the sale ends its CCA deductions?
options: Because CCA deductions are not tax deductible after year N
Because the sale proceeds are not taxed
The after-tax cash from the sale is received now, and the shields given up are worth less than that cash because they arrive slowly and decline each year
Because UCC always exceeds the sale price
questions.explanation: The lost shield is worth UCC x d x T/(k + d), a fraction of UCC. The sale delivers POD plus a tax effect immediately. Without other benefits from holding, selling usually wins.

questions.stem: A sell-versus-hold analysis at year 4 gives an NPV of +$31,005 for selling. What does this mean?
options: Selling now is worth $31,005 more, in year-4 dollars, than keeping the asset and its CCA shield
Holding the asset adds $31,005 of value
The sale price is $31,005
The asset will produce $31,005 of profit before tax
questions.explanation: The NPV compares the two strategies at a common date: after-tax proceeds less the PV of the shield lost. A positive value favours the sale.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly compares the three choices for the land in the Clean Air example?
options: Compare all three using each choice's accounting profit
Evaluate the project alone and ignore the land
Discount all three choices at different rates and pick the largest cash flow
Compare 'rent' with 'sell and buy back' first, then compare the better of the two with 'use for the project'
questions.explanation: Each comparison uses incremental NPV. The rent-versus-sell step shows what the land is worth in its best alternative use, which is the opportunity cost charged to the project.

questions.stem: Other things equal, a higher discount rate makes selling the asset at year N more attractive relative to holding it.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The lost shield is UCC x d x T/(k + d); a higher k reduces it, while the sale proceeds do not depend on k. The comparison tilts further towards selling.

questions.stem: Foothills Rail will sell its last idle crane at the end of year 5 for $24,000 and close the class. The crane cost $40,000, its UCC after year 5 CCA is $18,400, CCA rate 30%, T = 36% and k = 10%. If it keeps the crane it keeps claiming CCA on the UCC. What is the NPV, at year 5, of selling instead of holding?
questions.explanation: After-tax proceeds = 24,000 - 0.36 x (24,000 - 18,400) = 21,984.00. Lost shield = 18,400 x 0.30 x 0.36/(0.10 + 0.30) = 4,968.00. NPV = 21,984.00 - 4,968.00 = $17,016.00. Ignoring the lost shield overstates the gain; adding it instead of subtracting is a sign error.

questions.stem: An idle machine (CCA rate 20%) has a UCC of $33,177.60 after year 4 CCA. T = 35% and k = 12%. What is the value at year 4 of the CCA tax shields the firm gives up if it sells the machine?
questions.explanation: Value of the declining shield stream = UCC x d x T/(k + d) = 33,177.60 x 0.20 x 0.35/0.32 = $7,257.60 at year 4. Using k - d gives a nonsensical value; omitting T or the (k + d) divisor gives other wrong answers.

questions.stem: Bow Valley Aggregates owns an idle machine bought for $72,000 (CCA rate 20%, half-year rule). At the end of year 4, after claiming year 4 CCA, it can sell it for $41,000, closing the class, or keep it and keep claiming CCA. T = 35% and k = 12%. What is the NPV at year 4 of selling instead of holding?

It will be sold either at the end of year 3 for $22,000 or at the end of year 4 for $17,500; either sale (after that year's CCA) closes the class and the machine earns nothing meanwhile. questions.stem: Fraser Rentals must choose between two vans, one lasting 3 years and one lasting 5 years. Each will be replaced by an identical van when it wears out, and both provide the same service. Which method compares them properly?
options: Compare the NPVs of costs directly
Equivalent annual cost: convert each van's PV of costs to an annual amount over its own life
Compare the IRRs of the two vans
Compare the payback periods of the two vans
questions.explanation: The vans have unequal lives and a continuing need, so each needs to be turned into a cost per year. EAC = PV of costs divided by the annuity factor for the van's own life.

questions.stem: The equivalent annual cost of an asset is its present value of costs divided by the _____ factor for its life.
options: perpetuity
discount
growth
annuity
questions.explanation: The EAC is the level annual payment with the same PV as the costs over the asset's life, so it is PV/[(1 - 1/(1 + k)^N)/k].

questions.stem: Why can comparing the raw present values of costs of a 3-year machine and a 5-year machine give the wrong answer?
options: The raw PV ignores the CCA tax shield
The shorter-lived machine delivers fewer years of service, so its smaller PV of costs buys less
Raw PVs are in different currencies
The longer-lived machine always has the lower PV of costs
questions.explanation: Raw PVs are totals over different time spans. A 3-year machine will look cheaper even if its annual cost is higher. EAC puts them on a per-year footing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an assumption behind using EAC to compare machines?
options: Each machine will be replaced by an identical one when it wears out
Costs and the discount rate stay the same in future replacement cycles
Each machine will be used once and never replaced
The need for the service continues indefinitely
questions.explanation: EAC works because each option is assumed to repeat forever, so annual costs are the fair comparison. If a machine is used only once, simply compare PVs over the same service period.

questions.stem: Why does the PV of costs used in an EAC calculation subtract the PV of the CCA tax shield?
options: CCA reduces the firm's taxes, which lowers the true cost of owning the machine
CCA is a cash outflow that has to be reversed
CCA is already included in the operating cost
CCA raises the discount rate
questions.explanation: For a cost project, cash outflows are positive costs. The shield saves tax, so it is subtracted. The same is true of the discounted salvage value.

questions.stem: Rental van X has an equivalent annual cost of $7,240 and van Y has $7,905. What does this mean?
options: Van X costs $7,240 in total over its life
Van X is cheaper by $665 for each year of service, so it should be bought
The two are equal because EAC removes all cost differences
Van Y is cheaper because its life is shorter
questions.explanation: EAC is a cost per year of service. The lower the EAC, the cheaper the machine to provide the same service. The EACs, not the total PVs, are compared.

questions.stem: In PV of costs for an EAC with taxes, which pair of items reduces the cost?
options: The after-tax operating costs and the salvage value
The purchase price and the PV of the CCA tax shield
The CCA tax shield and the after-tax operating costs
The PV of the CCA tax shield and the PV of the salvage value
questions.explanation: PV of costs = purchase price + PV of after-tax operating costs - PV of salvage - PV of the CCA tax shield. Both salvage and the shield bring cash or tax savings back.

questions.stem: Computing EAC for two machines with unequal lives gives the same ranking as chaining each machine's cash flows over their lowest common multiple of years.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The EAC method implicitly assumes the replacement chain repeats forever, so it picks the same machine as a replacement chain over the lowest common multiple of the lives.

questions.stem: A 3-year machine has an EAC of $30,088 and a 5-year machine has an EAC of $29,138. Both will be replaced forever. Which should the firm buy?
options: The 5-year machine: it has the lower annual cost
The 3-year machine: its life is shorter and its PV of costs is lower
Either one: EAC is only for ranking, not for choosing
Neither: a cost can never be preferred
questions.explanation: The firm minimizes cost per year of service. The 5-year machine saves $950 a year. The shorter life is already accounted for in its higher annual figure.

questions.stem: Saskatoon Seed is choosing between press C and press D, both replaced forever. Press C costs $64,000, has pre-tax operating costs of $9,000 a year, lasts 4 years and sells for $14,000 (pool open). CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, T = 35%, k = 10%. What is press C's equivalent annual cost?
questions.explanation: PV of costs = 64,000 + 9,000 x 0.65 x 3.1699 - 14,000/1.1^4 - PV CCA (12,023.37) = 60,958.16. EAC = 60,958.16/3.1699 = $19,230.52. Dividing by N, using the other press's annuity factor, ignoring the shield or leaving the operating costs untaxed each produce a different number.

questions.stem: Press D costs $98,000, has operating costs of $6,500 a year before tax, lasts 6 years and sells for $16,000 (pool open); press C (4 years) has an EAC of $19,230.52. Same CCA rate 20%, half-year rule, T = 35%, k = 10%. By how much per year is the cheaper press cheaper than the other?
questions.explanation: EAC of D = 87,649.49/4.3553 = 20,124.97. Press C is cheaper by 20,124.97 - 19,230.52 = $894.45 a year. Differences of raw PVs ($26,691.33) mix different lives.

questions.stem: Prairie Haulage needs a loader and is comparing two models, each replaced by an identical model when it wears out. Model A costs $85,000, has operating costs of $12,000 a year before tax, lasts 3 years and sells for $25,000. CCA rate 30%, half-year rule, pool open, T = 30%, k = 11%. What is model A's equivalent annual cost, as a positive number?

questions.stem: Athabasca Pipe Works forecasts its project's cash flows in constant year-0 dollars, with no allowance for price increases. Which discount rate is consistent with those flows?
options: The nominal rate
The inflation rate
The real rate
The effective annual rate
questions.explanation: Flows in constant purchasing power are real flows and must be discounted at a real rate. Nominal flows, which include the expected price increases, use the nominal rate. Both give the same PV.

questions.stem: The relationship between the three rates is (1 + R_nominal) = (1 + R_inflation) x (1 + _____).
options: R_effective
R_nominal
R_real
R_after-tax
questions.explanation: The Fisher relationship compounds inflation and the real return. It is not the same as R_nominal = R_inflation + R_real, which ignores the cross term R_inflation x R_real.

questions.stem: The word 'nominal' has two unrelated meanings in finance. Which pair of contrasts correctly states them?
options: Nominal versus effective (compounding), and nominal versus real (inflation)
Nominal versus real (taxes), and nominal versus effective (inflation)
Nominal versus after-tax, and nominal versus pre-tax
Nominal versus risk-free, and nominal versus risky
questions.explanation: A nominal APR can be contrasted with an effective annual rate (compounding frequency). A nominal return can also be contrasted with a real return (purchasing power). The two are unrelated.

questions.stem: Which of the following combinations is NOT consistent?
options: Nominal cash flows discounted at the nominal rate
Real cash flows discounted at the real rate
Nominal cash flows converted to real by dividing by (1 + R_inf)^i, then discounted at the real rate
Real cash flows discounted at the nominal rate
questions.explanation: A real flow has no inflation in it, so a discount rate that includes inflation over-discounts it and understates the PV. The three consistent pairings all give the same PV.

questions.stem: Why is the real rate not simply the nominal rate minus the inflation rate?
options: Because inflation is paid out of the real rate
Because purchasing power is a ratio: (1 + R_nom)/(1 + R_inf) - 1 is slightly smaller than R_nom - R_inf
Because the real rate is always zero when the rate is nominal
Because taxes are paid on the nominal amount only
questions.explanation: At 10% nominal and 3% inflation, $1,000 grows to $1,100 while goods rise to $1,030: purchasing power grows 1,100/1,030 = 6.7961%, not 7%. The subtraction approximation drifts further for larger rates.

questions.stem: A firm computes a project's EAC with real cash flows at the real rate and gets a lower annual cost figure than with nominal cash flows at the nominal rate, although both PVs of costs are identical. Why?
options: One of the two calculations must contain a mistake
Real cash flows are taxed less
The nominal rate is risk free and the real rate is not
The real annuity factor is larger, so the same PV spreads into smaller annual amounts; real dollars are 'today's dollars' while nominal dollars are future dollars
questions.explanation: PVs agree because both methods are consistent, but EACs are expressed in different dollars. A real EAC is in constant dollars; a nominal EAC is a level nominal payment. Because the real rate is lower, the real annuity factor is larger, so the real EAC is smaller.

questions.stem: Maple Ridge Mills forecasts a project's cash flows in nominal dollars and has a 12% required return that already includes expected inflation. What should the analyst do?
options: Subtract inflation from the cash flows and discount at 12%
Discount the nominal cash flows at 12%
Discount the nominal cash flows at the real rate only
Add inflation to 12% before discounting
questions.explanation: The 12% includes inflation, so it matches nominal cash flows. Adjusting it again would double count the inflation effect.

questions.stem: A nominal cash flow received in year i is converted to a real cash flow by dividing it by (1 + R_inflation)^i.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Dividing by cumulative inflation expresses the future dollars in today's purchasing power: CF_real,i = CF_nominal,i/(1 + R_inf)^i.

questions.stem: Discounting nominal cash flows at the nominal rate and real cash flows at the real rate gives the same present value.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Both methods remove inflation from the comparison consistently. The nominal rate contains the inflation premium that the nominal cash flows also contain, and the real versions contain none.

questions.stem: Foothills Gas expects 2.4% annual inflation and its required nominal return is 9.5% per annum. What is the real required return?
